item.title: Lions create more than $35 million in cap space with restructurings
item.description: One day before their first game of the 2026 regular season, the Lions have cleared a sizable chunk of cap space.
item.content:encoded:
One day before their first game of the 2026 regular season, the Lions have cleared a sizable chunk of cap space.

And all that it implies.

As reported by the folks at Spotrac, the Lions have restructured the contracts previously signed by receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown and tackle Penei Sewell.

For Brown, the Lions converted $26 million of base salary into a signing bonus. That creates $20.8 million in cap space.

Sewell's contract had $18.6 million in base salary converted into a signing bonus. The move opens up another $14.8 million in cap space.

Most if not all veteran contracts give the team the ability to restructure the deal, every year. And it's a simple move. The chunk of salary that becomes a signing bonus is then spread over five seasons, with 80 percent of the payment being pushed into future cap years.

With the cap always going up, the move reduces the relative impact of those cap dollars, while giving the team more flexibility in the current year.

For the Lions, that means another $35.8 million in cap space available for 2026. Which officially puts them on the unofficial Maxx Crosby watch list, along with the Cowboys.

Crosby has a $30 million salary in 2026. And the Raiders already tried to trade him once this year, to the Ravens. If the season unfolds for Las Vegas in the same way that most seasons since 2002 have gone (with the exception of 2016 and 2021), the Raiders may decide to try to trade him again — and Crosby may welcome an in-season move to a contender.

item.title: 4 key matchups to watch for in Bengals vs. Buccaneers
item.description: The Bengals offensive line will face a fierce Buccaneers pass rush on Sunday.
item.content:encoded:
The Cincinnati Bengals will kick off their 2026 season Sunday when they host the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. It will be one of the best games of the opening week, as the Bucs are favored to win the NFC South, while the Bengals are expected to contend with the Baltimore Ravens atop the AFC North.

If the Bengals are going to start 1-0, here are four matchups they need to win.

Amarius Mims vs. Rueben Bain Jr.

Bain was the Buccaneers’ first-round pick during the 2026 NFL Draft. He surprisingly fell to the 15th overall pick and was not pleased. He will be playing with a chip on his shoulder when the Buccaneers face off against Cincinnati on Sunday.

For the Bengals, Amarius Mims is looking to continue ascending toward an All-Pro season. There are just not many offensive linemen with his combination of size and athleticism. The expectation is that Bain and Mims will be matched up for much of the afternoon this week. This could be a classic battle of the unstoppable force versus the immovable object.

If Mims can keep Bain from wrecking shop, the Bengals receivers should be able to feast on the Buccaneers secondary.

Dexter Lawrence vs. Bucs Interior O-Line

The Buccaneers interior offensive line consists of Ben Bredeson, Graham Barton, and Cody Mauch. All three players will have their hands full with the Bengals’ massive defensive tackle addition in Dexter Lawrence. Lawrence commands a ton of attention, and that will continue on Sunday.

If Lawrence can still create havoc on the interior with all of that attention, it is going to open up the rest of the Bengals’ revamped defensive line to make plays. Lawrence should help free up his fellow defensive linemen, but also allow for the young second-year linebackers to have opportunities to make splash plays against the run near the line of scrimmage.

Chase Brown vs. Alex Anzalone and Josiah Trotter

Chase Brown will be used in a variety of ways to get the ball in his hands. The Bengals would love to find ways to get him matched up against Trotter out in space as a receiver. Trotter was the Buccaneers’ second-round draft pick this past season. He is a classic downhill thumper against the running game, but was susceptible to giving up big plays against him in the passing game at Missouri.

If the Bengals can exploit that matchup this week, Chase Brown should have a massive week one game. The Buccaneers also added veteran Alex Anzalone this offseason at linebacker. Anzalone had previously played for the Detroit Lions.

Orlando Brown Jr. vs. Yaya Diaby

With Mims drawing the matchup with Bain a lot on the right side of the Bengals’ offensive line, it will be Orlando Brown Jr. going up against Diaby on Joe Burrow’s blindside. Diaby had seven sacks during the 2025 season. I would expect the Bengals to employ a lot of Drew Sample and Erick All over on that side of the field during this game.

Brown Jr. was credited with allowing 46 pressures, nine sacks, and 10 recorded penalties during the 2025 season. He has to play better this season in order for the Bengals to achieve the goals they want to achieve this season. That needs to start on Sunday against Diaby and the Buccaneers’ defense.

item.title: Indianapolis Colts Injury Report: Ins and Outs
item.description: Indianapolis colts injury report: who’s in and who’s out
item.content:encoded:
The Indianapolis Colts released their final injury report of Week 1 before their opening season game against the Baltimore Ravens.

Wide receiver Alec Pierce (heel) continued his week of limited practices. However Pierce has not been given a game designation so is ready to go on Sunday against the Ravens. Pierce may be on a snap count to ease him back into game time speed.

Safety AJ Haulcy (ankle) managed to finish off the week strong with back to back full practices. Haulcy, who is in line to start on Sunday has no game designation so should be fully able to go on Sunday. He is more than likely going to be rotated at strong safety with second year safety Hunter Wohler.

Defensive tackle Deforet Buckner (rest) and Grover Stewart (rest) both are fully available for Sunday despite missing practices this week, albeit due to rest days. Cornerback Charvarius Ward (rest) was limited to end the week but had mentioned to media earlier in the offseason he would be managing a back injury this season.

Quarterback Anthony Richardson (illness) Center Sedrick Van Pran-Granger (illness) both bounced back from illnesses this week and are clear to play Sunday although will be back up options are their respective positions.

Linebacker Austin Ajake (hamstring) is the only Volt to have a game injury designation and he is currently QUESTIONABLE to play on Sunday against the Ravens. Ajake missed practice with a hamstring injury late in the week and will likely be a game time decision.

item.title: Rams snap count review: Are the linebackers pulling their weight?
item.description: L.A. struggles defending the run in loss to 49ers
item.content:encoded:
After being out-coached, out-played, and yes, out-classed 27-7 by arch rivals, the San Francisco 49ers in their opening game, it is obvious that the Los Angles Rams have many holes to fill before they can begin to fulfill the high expectations that were bestowed upon them.

TST pondered about three philosophies that could be holding the Rams back. A fourth needs to be added. The thinking that undrafted linebackers are sufficient in today’s NFL. L.A.’s second line of defense was not only poor in Thursday’s loss, but has been a weak spot on a year-to-year basis.

With the Rams moving away from the 5-2-4 defense of the early Sean McVay years to primarily four-man fronts, line backers have to be able step into holes and stack/shed blockers or at least clog up running lanes. It is particularly so for the L.A. unit, since they are not gifted in pass coverage.

Names of players, their snap counts, and play percentage in bold.

While the Rams trio of Nate Landman (64, 98%), Omar Speights (30, 46%), and Shaun Dolac (19, 29%) combined for 15 tackles, by my unofficial count, only one play, maybe two depending on how you grade things, was made within three yards of the line of scrimmage. Their tackles were coming four yards or more past the line, they need make stops for loss or no-gain.

Defensive line 

Rough outing for the group as a whole, no one really stood out as having a strong game. The 49ers had a good pass plan, short and quick release, often one read. There was some pass rush pressure, but Purdy seldom had pressure up the middle into his face. S.F. ran the ball successfully both inside and off tackle.

Kobie Turner (43, 66%)

Poona Ford (33, 51%)

Tyler Davis (32, 49%)

Braden Fiske (29, 45%)

Ty Hamilton (12, 18%)

Edge

How quiet was this unit? Aside from Myles Garrett, who was on the cusp of solid initial game, a total of seven tackles, five which were of the assist variety and none for loss, one QB hit, and zero sacks. 

Byron Young (47, 72%)

Josaiah Stewart (28, 43%)

Myles Garrett (40, 62%)

Desjuan Johnson (15, 23%)

Safety

Quentin Lake (65, 100%)

Solid game for Lake, he’s at his best on underneath coverage where his smarts and experience can be put to use. Covering the slot doesn’t allow a lot of wriggle room, whoever lines up there is who you cover, but I’d rather see Lake tracking the bigger receivers and tight ends. Over the long haul, he is likely to struggle vs the smaller shifty/fast receivers.

Kamren Kinchens (52, 80%)

Appeared to me that two of the S.F. passing touchdowns came when he lost track of coverage. It’s simply inexcusable when the deep center fielder in Cover3 lets a receiver run right by him for a big play.

Jaylen McCollough ( 39, 60%)

Another workman-like effort from the ex-Tennessee Volunteer. He plays a smart, steady brand of football. Strong guy to use in rotations/packages. Got in a lot of special teams work, too.

Kamren Curl (30, 46%)

Curl was off to a good start, but injured an ankle and did not return.

Cornerback

Trent McDuffie (65, 100%)

Played about 25% of the time in man coverage and did very well. Liked the the way he stuck his nose in on run support as well as showing sticky coverage.

Jaylen Watson (65, 100%)

Drew Mike Evans and battled pretty well, albeit out-muscled on a pair of occasions. Still not a negative individual performance. 

Josh Wallace ( 7, 11%)

Hardly noticed him in the game. What was more noticeable? Emmanuel Forbes did not get a sniff on defense.

Special teams

Returns and coverage. Does anything else need to be said?

Quarterback

Matthew Stafford (51, 84%)

Rough game for Stafford, he seemed out of sync and his throws were off from the beginning. He seemed hell bent on throwing to his primary target, covered or not. How bad was it? Seven points was the lowest Rams scoring output in 75 games with Staff at the wheel. Staff did face a high 44% (11 of 25) pressure rate, but a handful of those came from him holding the ball too long.

Stetson Bennett (10, 16%)

Bennet did not look bad in the first real action of his career, but the 49ers had throttled things down by the time he entered the game. It was however, nice to see a Rams QB flash some athleticism and make some plays with his legs.

Running back

Kyren Williams (39, 64%)

On a day when the Rams needed an offensive lift, the snap share clearly shows that the offensive braintrust regards Williams and his serviceable duty as RB#1.

Blake Corum (14, 23%)

Hmm. Corum gets in for 14 plays and carries the ball on on 10 of them, no telegraphing going on there. Still, he showed good vision and feel for holes, while having enough burst to make good gains.

Ronnie Rivers (8, 13%)

Don’t want to cry over spilt milk, but wasn’t a mop up situation like this tailor-made for a fast back with natural running skills and power, but little pro experience? A guy like Jarquez Hunter. You can’t argue that it’s about special teams, because Rivers didn’t take a snap in those areas.

Wide receiver

Puka Nacua (43, 70%)

Would the Rams have had any passing offense without him? He made stellar grabs on two downfield passes, the Rams other completions were of the checkdowns and underneath variety.

Davante Adams (33, 54%)

He was open on occasions, but Stafford wasn’t close to hitting him.

Jordan Whittington (25, 41%)

Saw some good blocks out of Whit, but not really a an active part of the passing game. Did connect with Bennett later in the game for a catch over the middle. Didn’t add much in the kickoff return game. There wasn’t much Rams blocking, but he’s just not fast enough to work laterally.

Konata Mumpfield (16, 26%)

Quiet game for Mump, got his bell rung in the second half, but was able to return. I don’t see practice sessions, but it’s hard make a case for why Mumpfield is active over Atwell and/or Daniels. You could throw Brennan Presley in the that mix, too.

Tight end

Colby Parkinson (47, 77%)

My biggest complaint about Parkinson is his lack of physicality. He seldom, if ever, lowers the boom on smaller tacklers and drives them. Not a great blocker either. When the offense stalls, like Thursday, these things tend to stand out.

Terrance Ferguson (31, 51%)

Just one target where he was covered and badly overthrown. Although most fans want to see him as a weapon, it’s good to see him working as a blocker as well.

Davis Allen (21, 34%)

Had one reception on a check down and turned it upfield for a nice gain. Suffered a possible concussion on the hit and left the game.

Tyler Higbee (12, 20%)

Played mostly after Allen was hurt. Caught a couple of short passes, but lost a fumble on a peanut punch.

Offensive line

A hit-and-miss performance. Their run blocking was quite good and the pass blocking was just okay. Some of the pass blocking woes were scheme-related, too many long-developing routes. Stafford held onto the ball way too long on few as well. McClendon had some struggles with Bosa but got after it in the run game.

Alaric Jackson (61, 100%)

Steve Avila (61, 100%)

Coleman Shelton (61, 100%)

Warren McClendon (61, 100%)

Kevin Dotson (59, 97%)

Beaux Limmer (2, 3%)

The good news

As painful as it is to lose to the San Francisco 49ers, it is only one game and as pitiful as the pass game was, punching in that second half touchdown might have made a difference. No excuses though, the Rams came out flat and never got out of the funk. Who knows if the problem was the traveling protocols, a poor game plan, or just a pretty good ‘Niner team.

The key now is to work on weak areas. The Rams look to have the basis of a good run game and need to use play action off of it. The ‘Niners were very disciplined with their two-deep coverages and you can bet other teams are taking note. Sean McVay will need help make some room with play action and Stafford needs to be patient and willing to take the check downs and/or short stuff underneath. 

On defense, the edges have to dictate the terms of the opponents offense. Was there a single pressure by the Rams edge unit not named Myles Garrett? At the same time, if the edges are going to be routinely double-teamed, the interior will have to take advantage of the 1on1’s. Maybe the Rams will have to consider more man coverage, that’s what suits Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson’s past work and the deep safeties have to keep the action in front of them.

L.A. has 11 days to clean things up. As ugly as it was, all the problems are fixable.

item.title: New Orleans Saints vs. Detroit Lions Week 1 preview: 3 key stats
item.description: A data-driven preview of Saints at Lions, focusing on key stats and matchups.
item.content:encoded:
As enjoyable as NFL free agency, the NFL Draft, organized team activities, training camp, preseason, and 53-man roster coverage can be, nothing beats an NFL Sunday—and Week 1 is one of the most fulfilling and anticipated days of the year.

The Detroit Lions need this Week 1. They need it to wash away the ghosts of last year’s opener and fully bury the disappointment of last season for everyone in the organization and the fan base. And to get back to playing Dan Campbell football, the Lions will take on the team that helped cultivate Campbell into the coach he eventually became in Detroit.

The New Orleans Saints entered last season much like the narrative surrounding the 2026 Arizona Cardinals: written off and considered a favorite to land the first overall pick in the NFL Draft. But New Orleans’ season became a tale of two halves. The Saints were a plucky bunch that started 1-8 before finishing on a 5-3 tear.

That makes them a potentially dangerous Week 1 opponent—a team with a decent roster and coaching staff entering Year 2 that has built some belief in itself. That’s something Lions fans should be plenty familiar with.

Below are my three key stats and matchups for the Lions’ season and home opener.

Note: Unless otherwise indicated, all statistics are sourced from NFL Pro, FTN Fantasy, Pro Football Reference, or Pro Football Focus.

Staley’s resurgent renegades

A strong finish to one season doesn’t always translate to a team immediately picking up where it left off the next. But without any in-season evidence yet, it’s our best sample to judge what once-heralded defensive mind Brandon Staley’s defensive demons might be trotting out at Ford Field—even with the offseason losses of Deario Davis and Alontae Taylor, along with future Saints Ring of Honor member Cameron Jordan already ruled out.

From Weeks 10-18 last season, the Saints finished top 10 in defensive DVOA and top five in passing EPA, rushing EPA, passing success rate, and rushing success rate allowed—including an absurdly low 39.2% offensive passing success rate.

During that span, edge rusher Chase Young spent 98.9% of his snaps lined up on the defensive right side, while Carl Granderson spent 88% of his snaps on the defensive left. Young’s 36 total quarterback pressures ranked tied for 11th among all defenders, even with Micah Parsons, while Granderson’s pass-rush win rate jumped from 8.0% early in the season to 12.3%.

Even with the addition of Tyree Wilson, there will likely be a steady dose of Young against Penei Sewell and Granderson against rookie Blake Miller. That’s two formidable foes for the Lions’ newly entrenched bookends to kick off the season.

Kool-Aid McKinstry also became a completely different player during the second half of the season. After allowing a 120.0 passer rating, 68.1% reception rate, six touchdowns, and committing five penalties early in the year, those numbers plummeted to a 73.3 passer rating, 45.9% reception rate, two touchdowns, and zero penalties over the second half. McKinstry will enter his third season with confidence as the Saints’ CB1.

Also notably, linebacker Pete Werner improved from a 50.4 PFF defensive grade in the first half to 67.6 in the second. New third linebacker on the depth chart Danny Stutsman played 147 of his 204 season snaps during the second half and raised his PFF defensive grade from 59.8 to 74.3.

Then-rookie safety and now nickelback Jonas Sanker experienced a similar surge, with his run-defense grade climbing from 63.6 to 78.1, which ranked 13th among 67 qualifying safeties from Weeks 10-18.

It’s a relatively young defense that began to coalesce within Staley’s system down the stretch and is now being further entrusted to develop into a unit capable of helping guide New Orleans back to the postseason. This is a solid, ascending defense that will challenge the Lions and new offensive coordinator Drew Petzing immediately, providing a proper Week 1 litmus test for whether Detroit’s offense can get back to being a consistently dominant unit.

Heat up the gut

Stalwart Saints linebacker Demario Davis returned to the New York Jets for his third stint there after a wildly successful eight seasons in New Orleans. Replacing him is a Saints boomerang and the son of former Lions standout Luther Elliss, Kaden Elliss, who will play on the second level alongside Pete Werner and Danny Stutsman.

Elliss is one of the most disruptive pass-rushing off-ball linebackers in football, averaging 7.9 pass-rush reps per game over the last four seasons. During that span, Elliss has combined for 19.5 sacks and 42 quarterback hits—as many QB hits as Cameron Jordan—which rank second and first, respectively, among all off-ball linebackers.

Last season, Elliss recorded an 18.3% pass-rush win rate, fifth among off-ball linebackers, along with an impressive 17.6% pressure rate. That came one season after he generated a 21.5% pressure rate in 2024, which ranked seventh among off-ball linebackers.

Elliss is a one-man demolition crew as a pass-rushing linebacker up the middle. With Bryan Bresee out for the season and the Saints’ remaining defensive tackle group largely unproven or lackluster, Elliss and his attack-mode aggression will provide the toughest test for the Lions’ gelling interior offensive line of new center Juice Scruggs, third-year left guard Christian Mahogany (and possibly Ben Bartch), and second-year right guard Tate Ratledge.

Their communication and chemistry in the middle will be key to preventing Elliss from single-handedly submarining a Lions drive or two.

Aww, Shoughs

The two highest-rated recruits in Oregon’s 2018 recruiting class were Lions sixth-year left tackle Penei Sewell and Saints second-year quarterback Tyler Shough, with Shough intended to be the eventual heir apparent to Justin Herbert. Not everything went according to plan there. However, the Saints’ decision to take Shough early in the second round last year did, as the signal-caller positioned himself to potentially be their long-term answer after taking over as the starter in Week 9 and holding the job through the final nine games.

During that span, Shough ranked tied for third with a 69.2% completion percentage, ninth at 7.6 yards per attempt, and ninth with a 95.8 passer rating. Those are impressive top-10 metrics for a rookie quarterback in Year 1 of Kellen Moore’s system.

Not only were the Saints the fastest-paced offense in football last season, averaging just 27 seconds between snaps, but Shough also made quick decisions with the football once he became the starter. His 2.71-second average time to throw was the fourth-fastest in the NFL, with Jared Goff ranking first.

Shough was particularly successful targeting players out of the slot, with his leading targets there going to Juwan Johnson (28), Chris Olave (24), and DeVaughn Vele (12). On throws to the slot, Shough ranked top 10 in passer rating (10th, 104.6), yards per attempt (sixth, 8.8), completion percentage (fourth, 74.5%), and, most impressively, EPA per dropback (fourth, 0.45) among 33 qualifying quarterbacks.

Defending targets to the slot is one of the biggest mysteries for the Lions. Those matchups will likely involve some combination of Christian Izien (questionable) and Day 3 rookie Keith Abney II at nickelback, along with still-uncertain coverage responsibilities for linebackers Jack Campbell, Derrick Barnes, Malcolm Rodriguez, and Devin White, plus safeties Chuck Clark, Avonte Maddox, and Thomas Harper.

Factoring in the communication required to defend a fast-paced offense and quick passing game that frequently attacks the slot, this will provide a much-needed early-season test for Detroit’s middle-of-the-field coverage defenders.

All of that comes with one important weakness to keep in mind: Shough short-circuited under pressure. His 25.9% pressure-to-sack rate ranked 29th out of 33 qualifying quarterbacks, potentially providing an avenue for the Lions’ high-upside defensive front to feast against an otherwise above-average Saints offensive line.

item.title: Chicago Bears vs Carolina Panthers Preview: Bears need to slow Chuba Hubbard
item.description: The Panthers will try and impose their will on the Bears with Chuba Hubbard, so slowing him will be a must. We preview the game here.
item.content:encoded:
On her latest Making Monsters podcast, Taylor Doll previews the Week 1 matchup between the Chicago Bears and the Carolina Panthers with two individuals who know these teams inside and out.

First, she gets the skinny on Carolina by chatting with Alex Zietlow, who covers the Panthers for the Charlotte Observer. They break down the Panthers’ side of the ball, including the 2026 expectations for Bryce Young and how important the running game will be. Alex also shares thoughts on Caleb Williams and the Bears offense. Next up, she brings on our own Jeff Berkes to cover what Chicago will look to do and how the Bears can bring home a victory.

But back to Carolina…

Panthers running back Jonathon Brooks (2024 second-round pick) is completely off the injury list, and most assume he’s in line to be RB1, but Alex disagrees.

“The general fantasy football fan is like, ‘Well, Jonathon Brooks is like five running backs above Chuba Hubbard in the ESPN fantasy football drafts,’ whatever the case may be, and I’m trying to tell the world Chuba Hubbard is running back one,” Zietlow said. “Chuba Hubbard is a captain of this team. Like, he is probably the most important voice in that locker room outside of Bryce Young and maybe Derrick Brown on the defensive side. He is really important. In 2024, he had a 1000-yard season, and he didn’t even play every game due to injury. So, like, this guy’s really good.”

Hubbard and Brooks give Carolina a potent backfield, and in the 90-degree heat, they could be a factor against the Bears’ run defense.

item.title: Future Broncos: 3 Prospects to Watch in Week 2 of 2026 NCAA Football season
item.description: Here are three players Broncos Country should watch in Week 2 of the 2026 college football season.
item.content:encoded:
Week 1 of the NCAA Football season in the books. Last week, we took a look at a trio of potential first-round prospects that could be of interest to the Denver Broncos in the 2027 NFL Draft. This week we will cover three more players, with varying degrees of potential round placement, for the Week 2 slate of games.

Will Echoles — Defensive Tackle — Ole Miss

The defensive line is a key of the Denver Broncos. It’s a position they have acquired quality free agents such as Zach Allen, Malcolm Roach, D.J. Jones. Additionally, the have utilized some early round draft picks (Sai’vion Jones, Tyler Onyedim) the couple of years to address long-term.

It’s certainly not a primary need for the Broncos. However, Eyioma Uwazurike is in a contract season and D.J. Jones will be 32 next year and carries over a $14.5 million cap hit. With that in mind, taking a look at this year’s class of defensive tackles is worth considering.

Fortifying the defensive line is always a smart move, which makes it potentially in play if the right player is on the clock when the Broncos are picking next April. One player I’m bullish on is Ole Miss defensive tackle Will Echoles.

After a quiet freshman campaign, the former four-star recruit was a fifteen-game starter for the Rebels last season and notched 68 tackles, 11.5 tackles for loss, and 5 sacks. For his efforts, he earned AP first-team All-SEC honors and topped all P4 conference players with 39 quarterback pressures and 35 defensive stops.

He just turned 20 years old and there is no doubt his best football is ahead of him. He is a force against the run and shows great upside as an interior pass rusher. While had a bit of a rough outing in the Rebels’ close Week 1 victory over Louisville, Echoles should have a chance to dominate against Charlotte tonight. If he can put it all together this season, I would not be surprised if he wound up being a Top 15 pick next April.

Peyton Bowen — Safety — Oklahoma

The Broncos enter their 2026 season with Brandon Jones and Talanoa Hufanga slated as their starting duo. It’s an underrated group, and they also brought back Taylor Rapp who will eventually see time as a depth player for them this season. Though it’s important to note Jones will be a free agent at the end of the season, with Hufanga following suit in 2027.

As far as the rest of the players at the position, their roster is rounded out by Tycen Anderson, Devon Key, and J.L. Skinner. That trio has largely been career contributors on special teams—with their potential as foundational starters in the future unlikely. The team also has ‘26 NFL Draft selection Miles Scott on their practice squad.

I’ll admit that safety isn’t a premium position to address in the draft. History shows you can find quality starters at the position on Day 2, even as well as Day 3. One layer I think who will wind up hearing his name called a lot earlier than you think is Oklahoma Sooners standout Peyton Bowen.

After spending his first two years in Norman as mostly a backup contributor and special teams’ player, Bowen became a full-time starter in ’25 and was a second-team All-SEC selection. He posted 47 tackles, 7 pass breakups, and 2 interceptions. His size (5’11 and 200 pounds) doesn’t stand out, but his football play on the field does.

Bowen’s football intelligence and positional versatility are huge positives. I feel he has true potential as a single-high player but is also someone who has the chops to man down the nickel position in the NFL. That duality will be highly coveted by scouts and general managers in the coming months looking to bolster their franchise’s secondary.

He’s just consistent with most everything he does, which is a reason I’ll be keeping a close eye on him as the collegiate season continues. You can catch Bowen in action against the Michigan Wolverines in today’s early slate of games.

Vicari Swain — Cornerback — South Carolina

Fans might not want me to talk about the potential of Denver opting to use an early round selection on a cornerback in the 2027 NFL Draft, but here we are. I do expect one of Ja’Quan McMillian or Riley Moss to get an extension with the team. However, it seems unlikely both will earn well-deserved extensions.

The good thing is they have 2025 first-round pick Jahdae Barron already as an in-house replacement option for one of them. He has been cross trained at both the slot and boundary spots. While some were down on his lack of impact as a rookie, I’m optimistic about his NFL potential.

The Broncos are facing a situation where their All-Pro return specialist Marvin Mims Jr. may depart in free agency after this season. Finding players with his dynamic return ability are rare. That’s why I thought I’d bring up South Carolina cornerback Vicari Swain—who is an impressive cover corner who makes big plays on defense but is also one of the nation’s elite punt return specialists.

During his first two seasons with the Gamecocks, Swain (6’0”, 193 pounds) was primarily a backup player. Last season, he appeared in every game and had three starts. Even though he wasn’t a full-time starter, his impact (especially at slot) was evident with 28 tackles, 1 sack, 2 forced fumbles, along with 2 interceptions and 5 pass breakups. He also had 19 punt returns for 302 yards and three touchdowns.

This season he is poised to make a greater impact for his team. As of now, most outlets have Swain as Day 2 selection. While he doesn’t have a tough matchup this week, you can catch him this evening when South Carolina hosts Towson.

item.title: Big Blue View mailbag: Defensive alignments, expectations as season begins
item.description: The mail’s here! Questions, answers about the Giants with one day before the 2026 season-opening game.
item.content:encoded:
Richard Vitto asks: I was hoping you could clarify how the defensive line actually gets set up. Most of the time it seems to me that they play only 2 down linemen with 4 linebackers. Maybe to start a game or a possession they use a true front seven but without really tracking I really don’t think I see it that often. Can you give us a general sense of how often they are in a package with just 2 down linemen and extra dbacks? And when they are on that configuration who are the “starters” most often on the field?

Ed says: Richard, I could find and quote you numbers from last season. That, though, is pointless because the Giants have a new defensive coordinator and much different defensive personnel.

The “base” defense is considered a 3-4, with three down linemen with their hands in the ground. Again, though, that is kind of pointless. You will see some occasions where the Giants line up that way. You will see occasions where they line up with two down linemen and everyone else standing. You will see occasions where two edge defenders function as hand in the ground defensive ends, making the defense look like a traditional four-man front. You will see times when there is only one true defensive lineman. You will see times when there are none and an edge defender (probably Kayvon Thibodeaux) functions as a pass-rushing nose tackle.

Teams play defense nowadays according to down-and-distance, game score, and the game clock. It is all situational. It is impossible to give you numbers on how often different packages are used until we actually see it.

That said, the guys I would consider true starters in the front are D.J. Reader, Shelby Harris, Arvell Reese, Tremaine Edmunds, Brian Burns, Abdul Carter, and Thibodeaux. The safeties are Jevon Holland and Tyler Nubin. Dru Phillips is the nickel cornerback. I couldn’t tell you who the Giants will decided to start at the outside cornberbacks slots — it is some combination of Greg Newsome, Deonte Banks, Paulson Adebo.

John Brenner asks: It seems to me that the Giants have developed a troubling pattern over the last 10 or 15 years of not looking ready to play at the beginning of the season. I don’t have the numbers in front of me, but my impression is that they’ve lost the overwhelming majority of their openers and several times they haven’t just lost, but have looked completely unprepared.

Do the numbers and your own observations support that impression? If so, what do you think has caused it across different coaches and rosters? And do you see any reason to expect something different against Dallas on Sunday under John Harbaugh?

Ed says: John, have you not been reading the website? We have been covering this topic for months. In fact, we have been talking about it for years. I asked Brian Daboll about it before both the 2024 and 2025 seasons.

Most recently, it was addressed in this post.

Peter Smyth asks: This last week has been fan-torture. I can’t wait for this long, (but hope-filled), offseason to end and find out how good this team really is. National media, and even local writers and hosts are tempering expectations and predict slight or medium improvement. Often, they sound like they haven’t been paying attention to our team and are just writing us off. 

As a BBV zealot, I have convinced myself the G-men will go on a run this season like Washington in 2024 and the Pats in 2025. I’m asking you to be my Giants-fan-therapist. Am I nuts to strongly think this could be our year? Even a Super Bowl victory? Help me!

Ed says: Peter, you are certainly encouraged to be as optimistic as you want to be.

Something I keep saying, though, is that the kind of one-year turnaround the New England Patriots and Chicago Bears experienced last season are still the exception rather than the rule. I think if that is what you “expecting” in 2026, you are setting yourself up for disappointment.

Maybe it happens. I just wouldn’t expect it to happen.

When I made my game-by-game predictions, the most optimistic predicition I could make is 9-8. I still believe that. Maybe the Giants win six games. Maybe everything falls their way, and they get into double-digits in the win column.

I feel better about this team because I know the track record of the guy who is now in charge. I just can’t expect an overnight miracle. There is still a lot to be proven, and a lot of work to be done.

Doug Mollin asks: Saw a stat from Sharp Football that really caught my eye.

“The Giants were leading in games last year for more snaps than the following teams: Ravens, Chiefs, Bengals, Panthers, Vikings, Cowboys, Commanders, Browns, Buccaneers, Saints.”

Along with blowing 5 double digit fourth-quarter leads, it really makes me think the Giants could make a bigger leap this year than many expect. Could have had 7 wins last year with a little better luck, better coaching, better execution. What chance do you give the Giants to surprise on the upside over the predicted 7 win total? Is 10 wins out of the question?

Ed says: Doug, as I said above, it’s not out of the question. Neither, though, is being a six-win team. As I said above, I just wouldn’t go into the season believing that it is automatic that John Harbaugh is going to turn the Giants into a 13-win team right away.

Art Stein asks: To your knowledge is there any exchange of information or knowledge between the Giants and Rutgers. Historically, do coaches from Rutgers ask questions or seek information from the Giants?

Ed says: Art, I don’t know what kind of information you think Rutgers coaches might seek from the Giants. To my knowledge, there isn’t anything other than the standard exchange of information about NFL Draft prospects.

John McGruther asks: Do you know any of the words which the offense are using for their play calls and instructions, under the new coaching staff? I always remember “Omaha” being heard in the Manning years.

Ed says: John, if I did that would be a problem. The rest of the NFL would know them, too.

Submit a question

Have a Giants-related question? E-mail it to bigblueview@gmail.com and it might be featured in our weekly mailbag.

item.title: Browns keeping all 4 QB’s could pay off sooner rather than later as NFL injuries start
item.description: The Cleveland Browns still have all 4 quarterbacks around. Injuries around the league could lead to trade rumors soon
item.content:encoded:
The deadline for all 32 teams in the NFL to trim their rosters to 53 has passed, and Week 1 has started. During the first major roster decisions, the Cleveland Browns were one of the many teams that had difficult decisions to make. The one decision that surprised everyone is the QB room. There was a lot of speculation about how the Browns were going to handle the room, but the team decided to surprise everyone. Quarterbacks Deshaun Watson, Dillon Gabriel, Shedeur Sanders, and Taylen Green all stuck around.

Watson, Sanders, and Green are on the 53-man roster, while Gabriel deals with a back injury that seemed to pop up out of nowhere.

The Browns aren’t the only team that kept four quarterbacks around:

Could that decision soon pay off?

Excluding Watson, due to his contract, the other QB’s on this roster were the talking point in terms of whether to keep them or not.

Let’s start with Shedeur Sanders. Sanders, who is the most popular QB in the room and the backup to Watson has been discussed at length. From “if he will be the starter” or “if the team will cut him”, it’s always a conversation. The information that we have gathered surrounding Sanders is that the team never planned to cut him at any point. In terms of trading Sanders, the team may not have received too many calls before the season started.

Another quarterback that has been the talk of trade rumors is Gabriel. As the QB battle between Sanders and Watson continued throughout training camp, Gabriel found himself on the outside looking in. Gabriel’s ceiling has already been defined as a backup quarterback. Considering that the Browns took another QB in this past draft, Gabriel became the talk of many trade/cut rumors. The 53-man roster has come out, and Gabriel was placed on the IR, keeping him around.

Taylen Green, who the team drafted in the sixth round, was a tricky situation. Green is uber athletic but raw as a passer. Considering how Green looked in the preseason finale, if the Browns chose to cut Green the talented quarterback probably wouldn’t have cleared waivers, as it’s likely another team would’ve claimed him. Like Gabriel, Green had rare opportunities to get practice reps, but when he got them, he made the most of it.

Now, with two games in the books for the 2026 NFL season, the need for quarterbacks around the league has already picked up. Sam Darnold was injured in the first half of the first game of the season. While he’s expected to be back soon, the vagueness of his hip injury is something to monitor. Former Cleveland HC Kevin Stefanski is already starting his third-string quarterback, Cooper Rush, with Michael Penix Jr. and Tua Tagovailoa hurt heading into their first contest.

While Watson’s contract makes him untradeable, the Browns decision to keep all four quarterbacks around could pay off if teams continue to see attrition at the position around the league. Could the stability of Gabriel intrigue a team enough to fork over a Day 2 or high Day 3 draft pick and/or a quality player, once the diminutive QB is off IR? Could the upside and excitement of either Sanders or Green see a team make a play for a different Cleveland backup?

The Browns may not have the quarterback of their future on the roster, but it is possible the depth of options they have at the position means they have the quarterback of another team’s immediate future.

item.title: Which college produces the most NFL players? We examined all 32 teams
item.description: Alabama, Ohio State and Georgia form the top tier entering NFL Week 1, while LSU starts a second group after an eight-player drop from third.
item.content:encoded:
Heading into Week 1 of the 2026 NFL season, 202 colleges are represented on the league’s 32 active rosters as of Sept. 9.

USA TODAY analyzed roster data from NFL.com to uncover the college designations of the NFL’s nearly 1,700 players across every team’s active roster. College totals were calculated from the 1,689 players with a college listed.

Among school totals, leading the way with 57 players is Alabama. The Crimson Tide edges out Ohio State, which has 56 players. In third place is Georgia with 52.

It’s then a larger step down to No. 4. There, LSU has 44 players, two ahead of Texas and three ahead of Notre Dame. Michigan is just behind Notre Dame with 40 players.

Other top schools include Florida (37 players), Oregon (36), Penn State (36) and Oklahoma (32). The most-rostered FCS school is South Dakota State with six players.

Assuming Alabama holds its No. 1 spot through Week 1, it’ll be the 10th straight season the Crimson Tide has had the most or tied for the most players in the NFL.

Last year, Alabama had 60 players on Week 1 rosters, per the NFL, beating out Ohio State at 56. In 2024, the Crimson Tide had 61, while they had 57 in 2023.

Location-wise, the 202 schools are spread throughout the country with 48 U.S. states represented (the two without a college producing NFL talent are Alaska and Vermont). There are also two Canadian schools: nose tackle David Onyemata of the New York Jets attended Manitoba, while offensive tackle Theo Benedet of the Chicago Bears went to the University of British Columbia.

The heaviest-producing state is Texas, which has 16 schools represented in our dataset. Next is California with 11 schools, while Ohio and North Carolina have 10 each.

In total, 127 FBS schools are represented on an NFL roster. There are 11 such colleges without an NFL player, including Army, Northern Illinois and UAB.

The remaining total is made up of 49 FCS schools, while 26 are Division II, lower or outside of the NCAA.

Should the number of schools stay at 202 throughout Week 1, it’ll be a dip compared to recent seasons.

Last season, the NFL calculated that 233 schools were represented across the 32 Week 1 rosters, while 2024 had 234.

Those figures themselves were down compared to recent seasons, as 2019 through 2021 all had at least 240 different schools.

The 2026 figure is a USA TODAY tally of NFL.com active rosters immediately before Week 1, while the 2019-25 figures are the NFL’s official Kickoff Weekend counts. Because the figures were produced independently, there may be methodological differences between the 2026 count and prior seasons.

Methodology: USA TODAY collected roster data from NFL.com on Sept. 9, immediately before Week 1 of the 2026 season. Players listed by NFL.com with an active roster status were included and their college was credited as listed by NFL.com. School names were standardized where NFL.com used different names for the same institution. Four active players without a college listed on NFL.com were excluded from college totals.

For the map, schools were matched with CollegeFootballData to determine football classification and campus location where available. Missing locations were geocoded using OpenStreetMap.

The 2019-25 figures in the historical chart are the NFL’s official Kickoff Weekend counts and therefore may not be directly comparable with USA TODAY’s 2026 tally.

item.title: Cooper Rush is starting against the Steelers — but will it actually change the Falcons’ game plan?
item.description: Is the switch from Tua Tagovailoa to Cooper Rush really that big of a deal?
item.content:encoded:
Tua Tagovailoa’s back is tighter than a clam with lockjaw, and Michael Penix Jr. doesn’t trust his knee as far as he can throw it. It’s Cooper Rush time.

For some, this feels like the worst-case scenario for the Atlanta Falcons quarterback room, but is the drop-off from Tagovailoa to Rush really all that significant in 2026?

If we are judging who ran the offense more competently during the preseason, the answer is Rush. Yes, he had a rough outing against the Broncos, but Rush joined the roster only 15 days before the game. Since then, he’s shown command and the ability to keep Tommy Rees’ offense on schedule. His ability to pick up the playbook in that short amount of time is why he’s been able to stick as a backup in this league.

However, being a quarterback takes more than knowing the calls; when you look at physical ability and skill sets, Rush and Tagovailoa have been indistinguishable this summer. Neither is known for arm strength, and making plays out of the pocket is a crapshoot. Rush did show a slight willingness to push the ball compared to Tua, who had an ADoT (average depth of target) of 3.3, to Rush’s 6.3. Tua has an edge when it comes to processing, but he didn’t do a great job showcasing that during the preseason.

If this feels like a Tua slam piece, that’s not my intent, but it’s important that we establish how similar the two players are at this stage in their careers. These similarities are why I believe that Kevin Stefanski won’t have to tweak the game plan much, if at all. The staff clearly believed Tua could execute the offense better, but they can still ask Rush to run the same plan.

The 2026 offense was always going to run through Bijan Robinson, not the Falcons quarterback. He is the clear strength of this offense, a true one-of-one talent, and whoever is under center is here to manage the game. The worry for this offense, especially with Tua, is: what do you do when you get behind the chains or trail in the scoring column?

Many have been prepared to hold their breath on third-and-long this upcoming Sunday, and that’s not going to change with Rush. So Stefanski and Rees are still focusing on solving the same problem, which is a good thing. If the team had to adjust to a completely different play style at the last minute, I’d be more concerned about the product we’ll get Sunday. To be clear, I am still concerned to a healthy degree.

Rush won’t be expected to win this game with his arm, and neither was Tua before going down. This needs to be the Bijan Robinson show with an overdose of screens and quick-hitting passes. Hopefully, paired with complementary play from the defense, that’s enough to get the Falcons through Week 1.

item.title: 3-Point Stance: Undisciplined football derailed the Patriots’ chances against the Seahawks
item.description: Penalties and turnovers flipped a 10-point lead into a season-opening loss
item.content:encoded:
Seven second-half penalties and three fourth-quarter Drake Maye interceptions don’t comprise a winning recipe.

And on Wednesday night, despite holding a third-quarter 10-0 lead over the Seattle Seahawks at Lumen Field, the New England Patriots did just that, collapsing from self-inflicted errors. As a result, the Seahawks climbed back from the deficit to secure a 13-10 victory in the NFL’s season-opening Super Bowl rematch.

New England losing its advantage boils down to one overarching factor: undisciplined play.

Week One isn’t always an indicator of a team’s season-long performance, however. In 2025, the Patriots fell to the Las Vegas Raiders, who finished the year with the No. 1 pick in the NFL Draft and a 3-14 record, en route to a Super Bowl appearance.

Still, they’ll have their work cut out for them, getting back on track and planning around the loss of A.J. Brown, who will miss at least four weeks on short-term injured reserve with a high ankle sprain.

Ineffective execution

The team’s final offensive play stood out above the rest when examining the numerous poorly executed assignments. Those errors ranged from overall plays and coaching decisions to single-player performances.

With 26 seconds remaining on the game clock and trailing by a field goal, Maye forced a pass to Mack Hollins in the end zone, floating the target short, allowing Seahawks cornerback Josh Jobe to haul in the game-sealing turnover.

According to the Boston Herald, multiple Patriots revealed in the locker room that the late-game play was supposed to be a quick-game concept. Both offensive tackles cut-blocked Seattle’s pass rushers to promptly eliminate them on the play.

Instead, the plan broke down. Maye, under duress from right-side pressure and shuffling his feet for three seconds, missed an open DeMario Douglas for a first down and potential score, committing the takeaway.

Ultimately, in that crucial situation with a chance to kick a short field goal to send the contest to overtime, protecting the football is most important.

“Everything in the passing game is built on timing and built on protection,” Vrabel said on Thursday. “So, if [the play] is not where you want it and the timing of that particular play and protection, you just have to throw it away and say, ‘We can’t win it on this throw.’”

After an aggressive-minded play-calling approach that captured the 10-0 lead, New England shifted to a more conservative, bully-ball approach. The offense ran the ball 16 times on first downs and stuck with that strategy despite a 24% success rate in doing so.

On an individual scale, facing a long second-down snap, receiver Romeo Doubs dropped a wide-open pass in space that would have cemented a new set of downs during a critical fourth-quarter drive. One play later, Maye threw his second interception of the evening.

Doubs concluded the outing without a single reception, drawing three targets.

“I just wasn’t locked in enough on the football,” the former Green Bay Packer said after the matchup about whether confidence is a current issue for him. “The results speak for themselves. I’ll be better moving forward.”

The Patriots’ coaching staff is now tasked with regrouping and shifting the team’s focus towards what’s next. How the team responds to the loss will be pivotal.

“You either move past [the loss], or you go 0 and 17,” Mack Hollins said after the game. “I’d rather move past it.”

Drake Maye’s poor decision-making

That unsteady execution also extended into Maye’s performance, notably with his end-of-game struggles.

Possessing a two-score lead, Maye believed the offense had a “good” plan in place to chip away at the remaining time on the clock, thus limiting the Seahawks’ scoring opportunities.

But the 24-year-old’s turnovers allowed Seattle to take its eventual lead. It was a sequence not expected of New England’s young signal-caller.

“I lost patience, and it cost us,” Maye said after the defeat. “[They were] decisions that cost us the game on my part. I’ve asked myself to be better and realize it’s a long season, but at the same time (you) can’t have those [plays]. It was unacceptable … That wasn’t how I play football or how I want to represent my game and playing quarterback for the Patriots.”

Maye attempted to connect with receiver DeMario Douglas over the middle of the field in a third-and-long situation as just over nine minutes were left. However, Maye threw late and forced an interception directly into the arms of Seahawks safety Julian Love, setting Seattle up for a drive resulting in its go-ahead field goal.

His first turnover of the quarter came after another forced deep ball down the left sideline intended for Doubs in heavy coverage. The pass was tipped and fell into the hands of opposing cornerback Nehemiah Pritchett.

The quarterback’s errant passes may have stemmed from discomfort in the pocket. Even when the offensive line provided strong protection, Maye often appeared less settled than he did throughout last season, prematurely leaving the pocket occasionally instead of working around pressure.

Regaining his poise in the pocket is essential for the Patriots to replicate their 2025 offensive success.

Nonetheless, New England already has a foundation to regroup this upcoming week: a persistent belief in their young quarterback.

“We’re going to hold our head up high, and we have nothing but the utmost confidence in [Maye],” Vrabel said Wednesday night.

Stacking penalties late

And when the team prepares for its home opener against the Pittsburgh Steelers in Week Two, improving on-the-field discipline should be another priority.

Penalties contributed to the team’s collapse. Before the seven they were called for, the Patriots hadn’t been flagged in the first half.

Originally, New England took advantage of Seattle’s four penalties in the second quarter; that said, as the Seahawks cleaned up their play in the final frame, the Patriots evidently lost their focus.

After Seattle tied the contest at 10 apiece, rookie Gabe Jacas called for an illegal block on the ensuing kick return, pushing New England back 10 yards from its original spot. Then, on the following drive, Will Campbell was flagged for holding on the first play, forcing the Patriots into a first-and-20 situation.

The Patriots had control of the game but couldn’t maintain it or make the proper adjustments as momentum shifted. Now, they’ll have to prove that Wednesday won’t be a season-long trend.

item.title: Chargers vs. Arizona Cardinals: How to watch, start time, odds and prediction
item.description: Jim Harbaugh looks to stay unbeaten in season openers as an NFL head coach as the Chargers open the season against the Arizona Cardinals at SoFi Stadium.
item.content:encoded:
Jim Harbaugh wants his teams to finish seasons the way they start them.

If the Chargers do that, they’re going all the way.

Counting his four seasons with San Francisco, Harbaugh is 6-0 in NFL season debuts as a head coach. That’s tied for the most opening victories without a loss in league history.

“It’s September. It’s time to play our first game,” Harbaugh told reporters this week. “And I support no cause, foreign or domestic, other than the greatness of the Los Angeles Chargers.”

Read more:Mike McDaniel embracing life as the screen-averse sneakerhead guiding Justin Herbert

His team plays host to the Arizona Cardinals on Sunday, and oddsmakers see a blowout in the making. The Chargers are favored by 9½ points, the biggest spread of Week 1.

Despite a 2-0 start last season, the Cardinals lost 14 of the next 15 and wound up with the third overall pick in the NFL draft, which they used on Notre Dame running back Jeremiyah Love. The rookie is questionable for this game because of an ankle injury.

Their quarterback is no longer Kyler Murray, now in Minnesota, but Jacoby Brissett, who is on his sixth franchise — and seventh if you count two stops in New England.

This game is the “Mike” drop, if you will, with Mike LaFleur coaching his first game for Arizona, and Mike McDaniel making his debut as Chargers offensive coordinator.

LaFleur and McDaniel have history. They were young offensive assistants in Cleveland, Atlanta and San Francisco and both represent branches of the Kyle Shanahan coaching tree.

There’s a link too between Harbaugh and LaFleur. Both are younger brothers of other current NFL head coaches: Matt LaFleur of the Green Bay Packers and John Harbaugh of the New York Giants.

Key injuries

Cardinals: G Isisah Adams (knee) out; RB Jeremiyah Love (ankle) questionable; S Dadrion Taylor-Demerson (ribs) out; CB Garrett Williams (Achilles) out.

Chargers: CB Deane Leonard (abdomen) out; DE Tuli Tuipulotu (hip) questionable.

Cardinals vs. Chargers betting odds

How to watch and listen to Cardinals vs. Chargers

The Cardinals and the Chargers will play Sunday at 1:25 p.m. at SoFi Stadium. The game will be shown in Southern California on CBS and Paramount+. It will be available nationally via a subscription to NFL Sunday Ticket on YouTube TV. In Southern California, fans can listen to the game on 640 AM and 103.9 FM (Español).

Read more:From the ER to end zone: Inside Justin Herbert's L.A. life with his brothers

Who will win Cardinals vs. Chargers?

Quarterback Justin Herbert looks increasingly comfortable in McDaniel’s offensive scheme. The two new tight ends and a fresh Omarion Hampton at running back give the Chargers more firepower. The Cardinals’ coaching staff is a wait-and-see proposition.

Sam Farmer’s pick: Chargers 27, Cardinals 20

item.title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 1 Day Remaining
item.description: We continue our countdown to the Panthers opening the 2026 season against the Chicago Bears
item.content:encoded:
Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial.

#1. Cam Newton

How fitting that the player that comes in at number one on our countdown also wore the number one on his jersey. Serendipity. It’s Super Man himself, Cam Newton.

The Panthers and their fans endured a season of Jimmy Clausen to earn the number one pick in the 2011 NFL Draft. The team was almost guaranteed to take a quarterback, and the debate was between dual threat Cam Newton out of Auburn and the more traditional passer Blaine Gabbert out of Missouri. The Panthers elected to take a shot on Newton, and it couldn’t have worked out better.

There were all sorts of questions about Newton’s ability to actually throw the football when he entered the league, and the fact that he got very little runway into his rookie season because of the lockout only added to those concerns. He made his debut against the Arizona Cardinals, who clearly believed he couldn’t beat them with his arm, and lit them up for 422 passing yards and two touchdowns while adding a rushing touchdown on what would become his trademark super man dive over the pile on the goal line. He finished that season as the first rookie to ever throw for 4,000 yards, and he simultaneously set the record for rushing touchdowns by a quarterback with 14.

Newton continued to redefine the quarterback position throughout his time in Carolina. He paired high difficulty passing productivity with elite rushing efficiency and was one of the best short yardage ball carriers in the league regardless of position. His ascent continued into 2015, where he turned in arguably the greatest season any Panther has put together. He led the team to 15-1 record with the only loss coming just a few days after Newton welcomed his first child into the world. In that season, Newton threw for 3,837 yards and 35 touchdowns against 10 interceptions while adding 636 yards and 10 more touchdowns on the ground. He led a league best four fourth quarter game winning drives. All of that unsurprisingly earned him MVP and Offensive Player of the Year honors. He is the only Panthers in the team’s history to win either award. And all of that happened with Ted Ginn as his number one wide receiver.

The Panthers and Newton saw a major regression in 2016 after losing the Super Bowl. Newton missed a game with a concussion and was benched for the start of another because he didn’t wear a tie on the team flight. Derek Anderson started that game, threw an interception on the first play, and the Panthers went on to lose 40-7. The following week, Newton injured his throwing shoulder trying to make a tackle on an interception after wide receiver Kelvin Benjamin made a poor effort to catch the ball and then no effort to tackle the defender. That injury would dramatically impact Newton’s ability to generate velocity on his passes for the rest of his career.

Despite his diminishing arm strength, Newton bounced back to lead another hodgepodge offense to an 11-5 record and playoff appearance in 2017, but that season ended with a playoff loss to the Saints. After a strong first half of 2018, Newton took a shot to the shoulder from TJ Watt during a game against the Steelers. His play would rapidly deteriorate from that point through the end of the season before he was deactivated for the final two games to get shoulder surgery. He played just two games in 2019 before a foot injury ended his season.

After a year in New England, Newton made a triumphant return to Carolina midway through the 2021 season. He came in for special packages in a game against the Cardinals and was responsible for two touchdowns as the struggling Panthers pulled off a shocking blowout win over the then 8-1 Arizona Cardinals. Newton got more playing time as the season went on, but he was clearly not the player he once was. The Panthers limped to a 5-12 record after losing 12 of their last 14 games. Newton’s contract expired after that season, and he wouldn’t play another down in the NFL.

Newton’s career was very enigmatic in a way. On one hand, he redefined the quarterback position and reinforced how much of a weapon the quarterback can be as a runner while still being a threat as a passer. His impact and talent were undeniable. On the other hand, his consistency and counting stats as a passer could fluctuate, though there was a lot of context around that as well. The bulk of Newton’s playing career came with Mike Shula as his offensive coordinator. Shula never received any head coaching interest despite the success of his Newton-led offenses, and he never led successful offenses that didn’t have Cam Newton at quarterback. At the same time, Newton’s best wide receivers were an aging Steve Smith, a rookie DJ Moore, and Ted Ginn Jr. Newton was heavily reliant on Greg Olsen at tight end to be his true number one receiver for most of his career. He rarely if ever had a good supporting cast at the skill positions, and most of his career was marred by subpar offensive coaching.

While Newton’s career will go down as far and away the best we’ve seen at quarterback in Carolina, there are still questions about what could have been if the team did more to support him during his prime. Instead, he seemed to carry the weight of the offense on his own while the rest of the organization either did little to help or actively hampered what he was capable of doing. Still, he rose to the level of Most Valuable Player and took the team to a Super Bowl. Cam Newton is the best quarterback the Panthers have ever had, and the best player they have ever had. For that, number one in your programs comes in at number one on our countdown of the top 100 Carolina Panthers of all time.

item.title: Cowboys news: Malik Davis to miss extended time with hip injury
item.description: Here is today's Dallas Cowboys news.
item.content:encoded:
Throughout the training camp and the preseason, Malik Davis was easily the top choice to be the backup running back to Javonte Williams, but on Friday, he suffered a pretty serious hip injury. After years of hard work, tight end Brevyn Spann-Ford and wide receiver Ryan Flournoy earned contract extensions this week, and both have the potential to have breakout seasons.

DeMarvion Overshown is set to hopefully have his first healthy season in 2026, and he’ll do so as the Green Dot in Christian Parker’s defense. T.J. Bass will takeover the starting role at left guard with Tyler Smith on injured reserve, but it’s a task that he’s more than ready to handle.

Malik Davis out with ‘pretty serious’ injury – Nick Eatman, DallasCowboys.com

Malik Davis worked hard to earn the RB2 role for the Cowboys. Unfortunately, he was carted off the field during practice on Friday, and he’ll miss significant time with a hip injury.

The Cowboys offense suffered another big blow in practice Friday as running back Malik Davis suffered a hip injury that will keep him out of Sunday’s game in New York and likely a lot longer.

Cowboys chief operating officer Stephen Jones said on 105.3 “The Fan” on Friday that Davis had a “pretty serious” injury and could be out for a while.

“Unfortunately, I think he’s looking at a pretty serious injury that could take him out for some period of time,” Jones said. “We don’t have the final details, we’ll know more, but certainly so disappointed for Malik. Obviously tough for our team, but like anything it’s next man up.”

Spann-Ford, Flournoy reaping rewards of climbing NFL ladder with Cowboys – Joseph Hoyt, Dallas Morning News

Tight end Brevyn Spann-Ford and wide receiver Ryan Flournoy have both been grinding to find their place in Dallas for years. This week, they both signed contract extensions.

The fact the Cowboys extended both Spann-Ford and Flournoy on the same night is fitting. The two were both part of the 2024 rookie class. They share a trainer on the side. They both became pivotal players on special teams first before they rose the depth chart. Spann-Ford is now the team’s unquestioned second tight end. Flournoy is the team’s unquestioned third receiver heading into the season.

Dallas Cowboys Name Green Dot Role On Defense Officially Set For 2026 NFL Season – Josh Sanchez, SI.com

DeMarvion Overshown has battled his way through injury again, and he’s entering a contract year. He’s earned a very important role before the season starts, and that’s the Green Dot on defense.

Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer appeared on 105.3 The Fan ahead of Thursday’s practice, where he revealed that rising star linebacker DeMarvion Overshown has earned the green dot role.

Overshown prominently wore the green dot throughout training camp and the preseason, and will now carry those responsibilities into the regular season. For Overshown, it is a great opportunity to increase his stock in a contract year.

“It’s a process. Will there be multiple guys doing it? Overshown’s gonna be doing it quite a bit, but, again, with our different packages going into this game, we do have different guys that can do it, but D. Mo will be doing a lot of the heavy lifting,” Schottenheimer revealed.

TJ Bass ready, no stranger to what Cowboys need in absence of Tyler Smith – Patrik Walker, DallasCowboys.com

With the unfortunate injury to All-Pro left guard Tyler Smith, T.J. Bass is being called to step up. The good thing for the Cowboys is that this isn’t unfamiliar territory for him.

The waters-run-still demeanor of Bass has always worked in his favor, as does the fact that, this time, he’ll be asked to step in at a position he has a lot of experience playing — from his days playing for the University of Oregon.

“Yeah, I’m pretty comfortable with it,” Bass said. “I’d say like left guard is a lot easier for me to step in. It’s a little more natural because that’s all I played in college so, going back to that, it’s a little more natural for me. I’ve been mostly at center throughout the camp because this is the first year I’ve really had to back up center, you know?”

It’s obvious what Dak Prescott must do for the Dallas Cowboys to beat the New York Giants on Sunday Night Football – Mauricio Rodriguez, AtoZ Sports

The Dallas Cowboys have dominated the New York Giants with Dak Prescott as their starter quarterback with a 14-3 record. To keep that going, there’s something specially that he must do.

The single biggest storyline for this game comes down to one question: can Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott get the ball out fast?

The Giants may have question marks across their roster, but their pass rush is among the best in the NFL. New York boasts Abdul Carter, Brian Burns (one of the league’s most established edge rushers), and Kayvon Thibodeaux. Thibodeaux hasn’t lived up to his top-5 draft pedigree, but as a third edge rusher, he gives the Giants a serious rotation. Then there’s the X factor: rookie linebacker Arvell Reese out of Ohio State, also a top-5 pick, who will play off-ball but figures to be heavily involved in blitz packages.

Troy Aikman: ‘The sky’s the limit’ for 2026 Cowboys if defense improves over last year – SportsDay Staff, Dallas Morning News

Dallas has one of the best offenses in the NFL. After having one of the league’s worst defenses in 2025, they upgraded the unit significantly in the offseason, and that side of the ball holds the keys to a successful year.

“But I’ve said it also during the offseason that if the defense is better than they were a year ago — and I don’t know why I’m as optimistic as I am about the defense, I just feel like this defense is not only going to be better, I’m not saying they’ll be top 10 — but I think they’re going to be a group where people say, ‘Hey, this defense is good.’ Unlike last season. And if they are in that category, then in some ways it might be harder for the offense to be as good, even though they very well could be as efficient, if that makes sense. They won’t be playing from behind, the approach would change if the defense is better. But I think if the offense can go out and put the kind of points on the board that they did a year ago and the defense can make a few extra stops, then the sky’s the limit as far as what this team can do.”

item.title: Arthur Smith latest coordinator with NFL experience at Ohio State
item.description: Ohio State once again has a new offensive coordinator. Here's what to know about Arthur Smith, the former NFL coach turned Buckeyes' play-caller in 2026.
item.content:encoded:
For the third consecutive offseason, Ohio State's coaching staff underwent a significant change as Ryan Day had to replace one of his coordinators.

And for the second consecutive time, Day looked to the NFL for an answer.

Following Brian Hartline's departure for a Group of Five head coaching opportunity, Day tabbed former Atlanta Falcons head coach Arthur Smith to take over play-calling duties for a Buckeyes offense headlined by Heisman Trophy hopefuls Julian Sayin and Jeremiah Smith.

REQUIRED READING: Arthur Smith made his mark in a high-achieving family. Can he leave one at Ohio State?

Smith is the latest big name to come to Columbus to be part of Day's staff, following in the footsteps of former offensive coordinator Chip Kelly — a decision that kick-started this trend as it came when Day gave up his play-calling duties — and Matt Patricia, who willed the Buckeyes' defense into one of the nation's top units last season.

In Week 1 against Ball State, Ohio State's offense erupted for 56 points and 671 total yards, including 434 passing yards from Sayin, who finished as a Heisman finalist last season. Sayin threw three touchdowns, while two Buckeyes backups added touchdown passes of their own.

The game plan for Smith in Week 2, of course, will be a difficult one as the Buckeyes take on No. 3 Texas on the road, a defense that has held Smith rather quiet in meetings the last two seasons.

Here's what to know:

Who is Ohio State's offensive coordinator?

Ohio State's offensive coordinator is Arthur Smith, a former North Carolina offensive lineman who played primarily under John Bunting before going on to become an NFL head coach. Smith is the second former NFL head coach to serve as the Buckeyes' offensive coordinator, joining Chip Kelly.

His hiring at Ohio State marked a return to the college ranks for Smith, whose last collegiate role came as an intern at Ole Miss in 2010.

As the story goes, according to Joey Kauffman of the Columbus Dispatch — part of the USA TODAY Network — when Day reached out to Smith for his interest in the Buckeyes' offensive coordinator job, the former Falcons' head coach needed former Ohio State quarterback Will Howard, whom Smith coached as a rookie with the Pittsburgh Steelers, to confirm Day's number.

"I met him over the years," Smith said. "But didn’t know him well."

REQUIRED READING: Why didn't Paul Finebaum run for Senate? ESPN star opens up about decision

Smith spent the past two seasons as Mike Tomlin's offensive coordinator with the Pittsburgh Steelers, where he worked with quarterback Aaron Rodgers and helped lead the team to an AFC North title and a playoff appearance last season. Before his stint in Pittsburgh, Smith served as head coach of the Atlanta Falcons, further building a reputation for developing young offensive talent, including Bijan Robinson, Drake London and Kyle Pitts.

He landed his first head coaching opportunity after a successful 10-year stint with the Tennessee Titans, which ended with two seasons as the offensive coordinator to Mike Vrabel. In those two seasons as the Titans' play-caller, the NFL franchise ranked top five in the league in several categories, including total offense, rushing offense, red-zone efficiency and third-down conversion rate.

His time in Tennessee overlapped with Derrick Henry's historic season in 2020, when he became the eighth player in league history to rush for at least 2,000 yards in a single season. It also overlapped with A.J. Brown recording back-to-back seasons of at least 1,000 receiving yards to begin his NFL career, while recording 19 touchdowns in 30 games.

"He’s flexible," Vrabel, the now-New England Patriots head coach, told The Dispatch. "He’s adaptable. He can change with what's needed and have a pretty good pulse of what the offense needs, and when he was a head coach, what the team needed."

College Football Watchability Tiers: Ranking Week 2's schedule, best games to watch

Who did Arthur Smith replace at Ohio State?

Smith replaced Brian Hartline on Ohio State's coaching staff as the Buckeyes' offensive coordinator. Hartline left Ohio State following a three-year stint as the Buckeyes' offensive coordinator to become the head coach at the University of South Florida.

"It’s been great," Day said of Smith's addition and impact ahead of the season, according to The Dispatch. "He brings a great background of offensive football to the table. He’s been able to morph a lot of the things we’ve done with some of the things he’s done in the past."

Arthur Smith Coaching Career

Here's a full breakdown of Smith's stops throughout his coaching career including the college and NFL rankings:

  • Ohio State (2026-present): Offensive Coordinator
  • Pittsburgh Steelers (2024-2025): Offensive Coordinator
  • Atlanta Falcons (2021-2023): Head Coach
  • Tennessee Titans (2011-2020): Defensive Quality Control (2011); Offensive Quality Control (2012); Assistant Offensive Line Coach (2013); Assistant Tight Ends Coach (2014-15); Tight Ends Coach (2016-18); Offensive Coordinator (2019-2020)
  • Ole Miss (2010): Defensive Intern/Administrative Assistant
  • Washington Commanders (2007-08): Defensive Quality Control
  • North Carolina (2006): Graduate Assistant
