item.title: Julian Sayin could be trickiest QB prospect in loaded 2027 NFL Draft
item.description: Julian Sayin is no Arch Manning when it comes to his 2027 NFL Draft projection, yet the Ohio State star might be an even more puzzling QB prospect.
item.content:encoded:
In one of the most compelling early-season summits of prime NFL draft talent, one quarterback figures to yet again command the lion's share of attention.

At least a half-dozen potential first-round picks for the 2027 class will be on the field when the Texas Longhorns square off against the Ohio State Buckeyes on Sunday, with a horde of other likely early-to-mid-round prospects joining them. Texas edge rusher Colin Simmons, wide receiver Cam Coleman and offensive tackle Trevor Goosby all have earned universal acclaim as preseason All-Americans and projected top 10 selections, while Ohio State wide receiver Jeremiah Smith is viewed by many as the best player in college football and next April's premier draft prospect.

Of course, none will command the spotlight quite like Arch Manning. With his tantalizing tools, the Texas quarterback has become the focal point of what's expected to be one of the richest incoming crops of quarterbacks in years, even as teams try to square the discrepancy between the consistency of his performance and his overall capability.

His inverse – and perhaps an even more puzzling draft case – will be on the opposing sideline.

Whereas Manning navigated turbulence for much of his debut season as a starter, Ohio State's Julian Sayin never left much question about his efficiency after opening against Texas. His 77% completion rate stood as the third-highest mark in Football Bowl Subdivision history, and he finished second only to Heisman Trophy winner and 2026 No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza in passer rating (177.5) among full-time starters.

Yet for all his stability as a passer, the lone returning Heisman Trophy finalist presents a volatile range of possible outcomes in the NFL draft.

Sayin isn't mentioned in the same breath as Manning or Oregon's Dante Moore as a favorite to be a top-five selection, nor has he been widely grouped among in the next tier of passers that seems to carry less of a consensus. Of course, the ascent of Mendoza and fellow 2026 first-rounder Ty Simpson should prove that nothing is settled seven-plus months out from the draft. Another prolific campaign in which the junior smooths out the few issues that surfaced in his inaugural season at the helm could vault his standing with NFL decision-makers.

Still, those persistent and problematic questions of his pro projection could prove difficult for Sayin to answer.

Julian Sayin NFL draft scouting report: Ohio State QB's strengths and weaknesses

It doesn't take long for Sayin's biggest assets or his greatest liabilities to present themselves.

Precision and decisiveness are the hallmarks of the Southern California native's game. His accuracy holds to all levels of the field, as he led the FBS with a 62% completion rate on deep passes, according to Pro Football Focus, while he tallied an average depth of target of just under 9 yards.

Sayin also has remained a discerning presence behind center, throwing just eight interceptions and seldom putting the ball in harm's way.

"I think for Julian, you look for some traits that are extraordinary about him,” Ohio State coach Ryan Day said at Big Ten Media Days in July. “I think the first thing you recognize is his accuracy. What you don’t see, but I see, is his intelligence level. He can handle high levels of information. He’s highly, highly motivated. He’s really embraced this leadership role."

Yet much of the prevailing draft narrative on Sayin remains fixed to his pedestrian physical traits.

Sayin is listed at 6-1 and 214 pounds. Those numbers – perhaps generous, as schools tend to be with their figures – are a touch below what Simpson measured in at the combine and would surely make him one of the league's more modestly built quarterbacks. And while he's been able to reliably access the deep game thanks to his anticipation and touch, his pure pass velocity might not measure up to other prospects in this class.

Yet Sayin's biggest question mark and opportunity for growth might be in his response to pressure.

That concern didn't pop up in the opening portion of the Buckeyes' season. Through his first 12 games, Sayin took just six sacks. But in the Big Ten Championship Game loss to Indiana and ensuing College Football Playoff quarterfinal exit against Miami, he was sacked five times apiece. Sayin also threw three interceptions in that span.

Compounding the problem is Sayin's discomfort breaking structure. A pocket passer to his core, Sayin maintains a keen awareness of when the pass rush is trying to close in and will try to sidestep oncoming defenders. But he can struggle to embrace chaos when a play is being thrown off schedule. Pro Football Focus credited Sayin with just 11 scrambles in 2025 against 391 passing attempts.

"We know that that’s the X-factor that has to show up this year," Day said in the spring. "He’s aware of that and has been working hard in the offseason."

The early trend line has been encouraging. On a fourth-and-goal in the second quarter of the season opener against Ball State, Sayin notched his career rushing touchdown by climbing the pocket and taking off up the middle.

Sayin scrambles of the score 👀

Julian Sayin keeps it for the TD on 4th & goal.

Watch on BTN pic.twitter.com/W1wwEyTMDE

— Big Ten Network (@BigTenNetwork) September 5, 2026

The Ohio State problem

Operating within the Buckeyes' prolific scheme has no doubt been a boon to Sayin and his predecessors. Yet it's also complicated their pro evaluations.

Sayin has had the benefit of working not only with Smith, but also Carnell Tate, the No. 4 overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft. The two receivers have conferred a significant advantage with their knack for hauling in contested catches when they haven't left a defender in the dust.

That dynamic has amplified questions about whether Sayin is truly an offensive catalyst or more of a distributor who reflects his surroundings rather than changes them.

He's far from the first quarterback under Day, however, to face questions about transcending the Buckeyes' scheme.

In the lead-up to the 2023 NFL Draft, C.J. Stroud seemed to have a dichotomy similar to Sayin's: immaculate within structure but questionable when outside of it or dealing with pressure. His predecessor, Justin Fields, puzzled evaluators with the infrequency with which he was forced to make a secondary or tertiary read.

Sayin shouldn't be placed on either quarterback's trajectory, especially given that he's working under a different play-caller in Arthur Smith, a former NFL head coach and offensive coordinator who could better position his pupil for the pro game. But it's clear that a talent-rich and passer-friendly system helping accentuate Sayin's strengths also will create several unknowns whenever he enters the draft.

Julian Sayin's NFL draft stock could be unpredictable

Rather than any former Buckeye quarterback, the most notable touchstone for Sayin's draft stock could be Simpson.

The comparison isn't a perfect one. The former Alabama quarterback wasn't anywhere nearly as consistent as Sayin with his ball placement, and his lone season as a starter loomed over his evaluation. Simpson was also much more comfortable than Sayin in escaping the pocket to take off as a runner or buy second chances.

But the rough-sketch profile is similar: a modestly built pocket passer trying to convince teams that his pedestrian physical tools wouldn't be a significant hindrance.

Simpson's attributes sparked widespread skepticism after his uneven season, but he ended up being taken No. 13 overall by the Los Angeles Rams. A team that placed such a heavy premium on Matthew Stafford's ability to attack the entire field seemed like an odd landing spot for a young signal-caller who has more limitations. But Simpson's selling points were enough to hook Sean McVay and Les Snead into buying into him as a much-needed long-term investment behind center.

With an entire season ahead of him – and the ability to stay in college for up to two additional two years if he chooses – Sayin still has plenty of time to sway minds and perhaps even end up being taken in a comparable range to Simpson. If he doesn't make strides against pressure and in standing up to top competition, however, he could have a difficult time building a compelling case to be an early pick.

What is clear amid the uncertainty: There's significant work left to do, starting with Saturday's showing against Texas.

item.title: Commanders season preview: Stakes are high for Jayden Daniels, new coordinators
item.description: New contributor ShogunofHarlem93 breaks down what’s on the line entering an important a 2026 season for the Commanders
item.content:encoded:
Editor’s note: After posting some insightful stories in The Feed, Hogs Haven’s ShogunofHarlem93 has put together his first story for the main site. He breaks down why this Commanders season is so important for Jayden Daniels, new coordinators David Blough and Daronte Jones (and those that hired them).

Every season, I try to set realistic expectations for this Washington Commanders team. In 2024, my only hope was that Jayden Daniels would prove to be Washington’s franchise quarterback. And boy, did he deliver, leading the Commanders all the way to the NFC championship game. After an offseason of adding talent to a barebones roster, I had incredibly high hopes for 2025. Instead, the season was completely gutted. Injuries, poor decision making and uncompetitive games dragged Washington down to a massive low point, erasing a decade’s worth of renewed optimism. It made last year incredibly hard to stomach. 

Head coach Dan Quinn saw the writing on the wall and let both of his coordinators go. While most head coaches in his position would hire experienced retreads to save their own skins, Quinn took a massive gamble. He brought in two newcomers: Daronte Jones and David Blough. We have absolutely no clue how this will translate when the games actually matter. The stakes are incredibly high, and every single storyline this year feels like an unprecedented gamble. 

Will the real Jayden Daniels stand up 

Jayden Daniels entered the league with a clear mission statement: prove he was the best quarterback in the 2024 NFL draft class. He shattered records and dragged this franchise somewhere it hadn’t been in over 30 years — the NFC Championship Game. Even though they were ultimately handled by a dominant Philly team that went on to win the Super Bowl, the foundation seemed set. Yet, despite the optimism surrounding his progression, the “sophomore slump” narrative still loomed. I blindly dismissed it at the time, firmly believing a slump was impossible because his rookie year was a tale of two entirely different Jaydens. 

Early in 2024, then-offensive coordinator Kliff Kingsbury relied heavily on first-down screens, RPOs and vertical concepts. At one point, Washington ran an absurd 35% of their first-down plays as screens to protect a highly suspect offensive line. The faster Jayden got the ball out, the better.  

But in Week 11, the Eagles completely exposed the game plan. Philly squeezed the offense’s lateral spacing and dared Daniels to attack the intermediate middle of the field. While most rookie quarterbacks could’ve hit a wall and coordinators could’ve waited until the offseason to adjust, Washington adapted immediately. Over the following weeks, they challenged the toughest part of the field — the 6-to-10-yard intermediate middle. Their screen frequency plummeted from 35% to 21%, the vertical deep shots were scaled back and they completely rebuilt the offense on the fly without losing momentum. It is impossible to overstate how impressive it was for a rookie to handle that mental adjustment.  

That mid-season pivot is exactly what made 2025 so incredibly frustrating. We can talk about the injuries and the lackluster supporting cast — points that have been discussed ad nauseam — but when he was on the field, the performance simply wasn’t there. His completion percentage tanked by an alarming 9%. There were costly underthrows, balls skipped into the dirt and while the playmakers around him offered little help, the regression from his rookie brilliance was surreal. 

To put a 9% completion percentage drop into historical perspective, look at how similar drop-offs impacted other notable quarterbacks: 

 
Daniels faces an uphill battle, but history shows a recovery isn’t impossible — especially when you look at guys like Joe Burrow or Kurt Warner who weathered the storm. What makes his current situation so fascinating is that he is learning a brand-new offense simultaneously. Transitioning to a true pro-style system after years in spread and RPO-heavy schemes is a massive hurdle, but the buzz out of training camp has been incredibly positive regarding his mental processing. He took over 500 snaps in camp, an intensive workload designed to fast-track his comfort level. Whether that practice volume translates to wins remains to be seen, but the foundation is there.

If JD5 can bounce back and replicate or surpass his rookie efficiency, watch out: he’ll vault right back into the top-10, if not the top-5 quarterback conversation. 

Defense? DEFENSE!! 

I can join the crowd and rag on former defensive coordinator Joe Whitt Jr. all day, but let’s be real — he wasn’t the sole reason this defense was completely awful. When your best pass rusher is a nearly 40-year-old Von Miller, you have fundamental problems. The personnel was a total mess.  

An old, slow defense will get absolutely ripped to shreds in today’s NFL. Even when Quinn took over the defensive play-calling duties they were still getting dismantled, proving a massive overhaul was needed. To Quinn’s credit, he recognized his own limitations, stepped back and brought in a defensive coordinator whose system is a complete departure from the scheme Quinn ran his entire career. 

Enter Daronte Jones. Outside of his brief stint calling plays at LSU, he’s a first-time NFL coordinator tasked with bringing a chaotic, Brian Flores-style scheme to Washington. To give him a fighting chance, management went all-in, injecting $165.8 million into that side of the ball — the sixth-highest defensive spend in the league. They completely reshaped the roster by signing Odafe Oweh, Tim Settle, K’Lavon Chaisson, Nick Cross and Leo Chenal, while using the draft to secure young talent like Sonny Styles and Joshua Josephs. 

With up to eight new starters, this unit simply has to outperform the disasters of the past three defensive seasons. Everything will live and die with the defensive line. For the last two years, this team was hellbent on blitzing heavy on first and second down to force third-and-long situations. The fatal flaw? They kept giving up first downs anyway, not to mention working with a completely awful run defense. The new additions must restore order in the trenches and finally unlock the underperforming duo of Daron Payne and Javon Kinlaw. With a brand-new scheme and a completely reconstructed starting lineup, this defense is one of the biggest mysteries in the league. 

New-ish Sheriff in Town  

When Kliff Kingsbury was initially hired, I wasn’t a fan. I believed his offense was inherently predictable and destined to hit a proverbial wall every season. While his explosive 2024 campaign proved me wrong, he unfortunately reverted to those same stubborn play-calling habits in 2025. His firing wasn’t a shock, though I did assume he’d get one final year to redeem himself. Instead, Quinn opted for a total philosophical shift. Despite the established offensive minds available on the market, Quinn took a massive gamble by appointing rookie offensive coordinator David Blough. As a former journeyman quarterback, Blough played under the likes of Kingsbury, Kevin O’Connell and Ben Johnson, giving him a fascinating blend of modern offensive influences. 
Still, Blough remains the team’s biggest wild card. He is being thrown directly into the fire with zero prior experience building a weekly NFL game plan.

Making matters even more precarious, Washington hired Darnell Stapleton, a coach with no previous experience leading an NFL offensive line room. Given this infrastructure, the offense is bound to experience severe growing pains as the new staff figures out how to establish a baseline rhythm. 

Training camp reports have been a mixed bag, particularly regarding the line’s consistency. However, the upgraded weaponry around Jayden Daniels provides genuine reason for optimism. Stefon Diggs and Chig Okonkwo completely reshape the passing game alongside Terry McLaurin, while dynamic pieces like Antonio Williams offer an intriguing mismatch chess piece. The ceiling for this group is incredibly exciting, but the season ultimately hinges on whether this unproven coaching staff can get the offensive line to perform consistently. 

I am not, and will not, put a concrete record prediction on file, but this season is undeniably pivotal for the Adam Peters and Dan Quinn regime. Both of their seats are getting hot. They need a playoff appearance or heads will roll once again. For Daniels, this season has to serve as a definitive reminder of the elite player he proved he could be during his historic rookie campaign. If everything clicks, this roster absolutely has the talent to be a playoff team. But if the cracks begin to show again, fans will be forced to endure yet another painful reboot in a never-ending cycle of heartbreak. To borrow a phrase from De La Soul, the stakes are indeed high.

item.description: Mike Tomlin says the best team he coached wasn’t the one that won the Super Bowl.
item.content:encoded:
Mike Tomlin revealed the best team he ever coached in a recent interview with the Today Show — and according to the former Steelers head coach, it’s not the 2008-09 team that won Super Bowl XLIII.

“The best team I coached, probably, didn’t win,” Tomlin said. “Probably in the mid-teens, 2015-16. Denver won it that year with Peyton (Manning).”

The 2015 Steelers went 10-6, led by the league’s fourth-best scoring offense averaging 26.4 points per game. The team finished second in the AFC North, winning in the wild card round over the Cincinnati Bengals but falling in the divisional round to the eventual Super Bowl Champion Broncos.

The Steelers fell in Denver, 23-16, in a game wide receiver Antonio Brown, running back Le’Veon Bell, and offensive linemen Kelvin Beachum and Maurkice Pouncey missed with injury.

“Sometimes, man, things don’t come together for you,” Tomlin said.

The Pittsburgh offense put up strong numbers that year. Quarterback Ben Roethlisberger recorded 3,938 passing yards with 21 touchdowns and 16 interceptions in just 11 starts. Wide receiver Antonio Brown put up a 136-catch, 1,834-yard season with 10 touchdowns. Wide receivers Markus Wheaton and Martavis Bryant each recorded well over 700 receiving yards each, with tight end Heath Miller adding another 535.

The Pittsburgh run game that year was led by DeAngelo Williams (907 rushing yards in 10 starts) and Bell (556 yards in six starts). The starting offensive line was made up of Beachum, Ramon Foster, Pouncey, David DeCastro and Marcus Gilbert.

On defense, the 2015 Steelers finished 11th in the NFL that year in scoring, led by a core of Cam Heyward, Stephon Tuitt, Lawrence Timmons, James Harrison and Ryan Shazier.

Tomlin was reportedly more emotional than usual following the loss in Denver.

“That team? That team was as talented as any team I’ve ever been around,” Tomlin told the Today Show. “We had the goods. But that’s what I love and respect about football, man. It’s a single elimination tournament. It’s not best out of seven. We went into that stadium that day without our No. 1 running back and without our No. 1 wideout, and we suffered the consequences of it. That’s life.

“But if you ask me the best team I’ve been around, it would probably be that team.”

item.description: New York Giants headlines for Saturday
item.content:encoded:
Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to as the John Harbaugh Era starts tomorrow.

John Harbaugh not leaving anything to chance as his Giants era begins | The Record

This was the early evening before the New York Giants began training camp at The Greenbrier Resort and John Harbaugh was walking the grounds for the first time.

The head coach and several team officials were admiring the picturesque setting with the mountains of West Virginia as the backdrop when someone half-jokingly suggested that the practice fields looked longer than 120 yards.

Harbaugh on why Giants were the right fit

Harbs Weekly: Time to get a gauge on the Giants | Giants.com

Q: That was the start of his era with you, and now the same begins with Jaxson Dart. Where is the line between the importance of the quarterback-head coach relationship and him just being one of 53 on the roster?

Harbaugh: To me it’s both, but everybody understands it. He is one of 53. He’s part of the team. He’s a teammate. He’s a player. The guys like Jaxson, Joe [Flacco], Lamar [Jackson], they all understand that so well. That’s why the players love them so much. But the other side of the coin is he’s the quarterback. He’s got to know the most. He’s got to do the most. He has the most impact probably on the game of anybody. So, that part of it is just kind of understood. But those guys, man, they’ve been doing it their whole life. They embrace it.

NFC East roundtable: Eagles, Cowboys, Commanders enter critical seasons; Giants seek new culture | The Athletic

Who’s the player not enough people are talking about who’s going to make a big impact for the team you cover?

Carroll: Isaiah Likely was one of the Giants’ biggest free-agent acquisitions, as the tight end signed a three-year, $40 million deal. That type of deal doesn’t usually lead to a player not being talked about enough. However, in a New York media market adoring the Odell Beckham Jr. reunion, while at the same time fixating on Malik Nabers’ return from a torn ACL, Likely has quietly been putting in the work becoming quarterback Jaxson Dart’s go-to pass catcher. As my colleague Dan Duggan noted, Likely was Dart’s favorite target this summer with 44 catches in 11-on-11 team periods during camp. With or without Nabers’ return in Week 1, Likely figures to be a big piece of this offense.

After years of losing, Giants star says, ‘My urgency level is high. This doesn’t last forever’ | NJ.com

Given how small an NFL player’s career window typically winds up being, how eager is Burns to win?

“Oh, I’ve been at that point…I don’t really give a f— about surprising nobody,” he said. “I’m just focused on our team, our opponents and get a dub as many times as we can throughout the season — and getting to the big dance. Surprising people and putting the world on notice? I don’t give a f— about none of that. Not anymore.

“I used to want to prove people wrong and prove this and prove that. But I got to a point where it’s like now, bro, people are going to say something regardless of whether you’re good or whether you’re bad. So it really doesn’t matter. The only thing that matters is the work that’s in front of you. I’m not doing this to prove to nobody else. I do it more so to prove to my guys and myself that we can win.”

Giants hope new D-coordinator will be one to finally stop Dak Prescott | New York Post

The next coordinator in line is Dennard Wilson, who will be making his Giants debut Sunday and he doesn’t care about Giants-Cowboys history.

“We’re going to be unapologetic on how we play,” he said. “We’re going to be decisive in what we do. We’re going to play with an edge. We’re going to play with toughness. We’re going to bring violence. That’s our M.O. That’s how the guys have been going out — doing their work every day, their daily business. And that’s how we’re going to play.”

NFL Week 1 picks, predictions, schedule, odds, fantasy tips | ESPN.com

What we’re hearing on the Giants: It’s the first game of the John Harbaugh era. It’s QB Jaxson Dart’s first opening game start in the NFL. The Giants say they believe they have their signal-caller and coach and that it will lead to wins. Immediately. “I want to do something special. And all the guys in the locker room are, too. We’re starving for this,” Dart said.

Bold prediction: Giants rookie WR Malachi Fields will lead the team in receiving yards. It remains to be seen exactly how close to 100% Malik Nabers (knee) is. Fields had a great camp and the Cowboys CBs DaRon Bland and Cobie Durant are beatable.

Kurt Warner on being benched for Eli

Lawrence Taylor Leads Six Giants Named to Sporting News’ 140 Greatest Players Ever | SI.com

Taylor ranked fourth on Iyer’s list, going down as the greatest defensive player in league history. The only other defensive players included in the top ten were Reggie White (5th) and Aaron Donald (8th). Only Jim Brown, Jerry Rice, and Tom Brady ranked ahead of Taylor. Michael Strahan is the most recent Giants player to make Iyer’s list. The NFL’s sixth-leading sack-getter ranked 81st.

Most of the Giants players included came long before the modern era of the NFL. Mel Hein, who played for Big Blue from 1931 to 1945, was the earliest player to make the cut, ranking 90th. Hein played both center and linebacker and remains the only offensive lineman in NFL history to win MVP. Linebacker Sam Huff (ranked 136th), offensive tackle Roosevelt Brown (98th), and safety Emlen Tunnell (76th) all played together for the Giants in the 1950s, winning a championship in 1956. Each player is a member of the Pro Football Hall of Fame.

item.content:encoded:
“Waiting for injury update” news days are the worst. At least this particular situation is 1) a Saturday after a big Thursday win 2) has plenty of exciting highlights from said win to dig through. I’ve been enjoying reading more about how Shanahan is using “rounded motions” with Kyle Juszczyk, all the ways he was sending random players to chip Myles Garrett, and the different superhero plays that Fred Warner was making all game. 

49ers vs. Rams PFF grades: Best and worst from the game, plus snap counts
“Right tackle Colton McKivitz’s 75.1 offensive grade was the highest among 49ers offensive linemen, while left guard Connor Colby’s 53.5 offensive grade was the lowest.”

Kawakami: The 49ers’ obsession, commitment, and triumphant Australia Plan (paywall)
“We’ll see what happens next; maybe the 49ers will fall into a funk after spending so much time in Australia and expending so much energy to get this win. But they’ve got two extremely winnable home games in the next two weeks (Miami and Arizona) before the season starts to get serious again.

I’d imagine that we probably won’t really know much more about the 49ers’ full-season biorhythms until the Oct. 11 game in Seattle. That’s when we’ll probably really know if the 49ers played this 100% right or are set to go through some body-clock payback.”

49ers enjoy family reunion in rout of Rams: ‘It felt like I never left’ (paywall)
“During the 16-hour flight to Australia, the 49ers had strict instructions on when to sleep, how many ounces of fluids to drink, when to put their window shades up and how often to slip on blue-light glasses.

After rolling over their division rivals, the plan for the flight back was more simple.

“Party it up,” Warner said.”

49ers’ game review: How Kyle Shanahan dinked, dunked and KO’d the Rams’ vaunted defense (paywall)
“Shanahan uses Juszczyk in motion creatively. On Thursday, Juszczyk was often aligned as a tight end before he looped across the line of scrimmage, often running a half circle, allowing him to have a running head start as a 235-pound lead blocker.

On the 49ers’ first offensive snap, Juszczyk lined up outside Williams, went in motion and led the way for a running back Christian McCaffrey’s 6-yard burst up the middle. Six plays later, Juszczyk on the right side, ran across the formation and cleared out safety Kam Curl on a 5-yard screen to running back Kaelon Black on the left side.

Juszczyk’s banana-shaped motions created social-media buzz. But they aren’t new. In fact, Juszczyk was doing it against the Rams last season in a loss in November. After the in-motion Juszczyk looped around QB Mac Jones, who was in shotgun formation, to serve a full-speed lead blocker on an 11-yard run, Fox analyst Tom Brady commented on Shanahan’s play design.

“In 25 years of watching football, I’ve never seen that exact concept,” Brady said.”

item.title: Eagles notebook: Why LBs coach is so excited about this year's duo
item.description: In the latest Eagles notebook: Dontayvion Wicks talks about his connection with Jalen Hurts, Bobby King is excited about his linebackers and more.
item.content:encoded:
Eagles notebook: Why LBs coach is so excited about this year's duo  originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Is Jihaad Campbell going to make a big jump in the second year of his NFL career?

The Eagles sure hope so.

Campbell had a perfectly fine rookie season as a first-round pick in 2025, but did lose his starting job when Nakobe Dean returned from injury. But now Dean is a Raider and Campbell is back in the starting lineup with Zack Baun in the middle of Vic Fangio’s defense. And Campbell is reaping the benefits of Year 2.

“The game is slowing down,” linebackers coach Bobby King said recently. “When teams are doing all this stuff, motion and all that, you’re not seeing so much and you’re able to react, you’re able to get off blocks and you’re able to play football. It’s done that so far and I can’t wait to see it next week.”

Baun and Campbell spent all training camp next to each other with the first-team defense and actually got a chance to start eight games with each other last season. King seems excited about the versatility of both players in the middle of this defense. Baun is 29 now and has been a Pro Bowler in each of his first two seasons with the Eagles. His 2025 wasn’t as splashy as his 2024, but he was still really good.

“The thing people don’t talk about last year with Zack was he played through a bunch of stuff,” King revealed. “Not going to get into that, but didn’t miss a snap barely, played through some stuff and was a war daddy for me. Main thing is just staying out there and being healthy. The rest will take care of itself.”

Time well spent

In the five months since Dontayvion Wicks got traded to the Eagles, he has spent a ton of time catching passes from Jalen Hurts — both in practice and on their own.

That was time well spent.

“I think the chemistry is built,” Wicks said. “It’s been a long way through camp and through the summer, the offseason. I think that’s the little things that people don’t see, that come to light when it’s time to go out on the field. 

“At times during camp, you see it. You see that chemistry build. And that’s not just from going out at practice. That’s being off the field and doing things off the field, away from the cameras. I would say putting that time in has helped with the chemistry and helped us build a better relationship, getting to know each other. I think that’s the biggest part.”

Wicks, 25, spent his first three seasons in Green Bay but was more of a rotational role player. In three years with the Packers, Wicks caught 108 passes for 1,328 yards and 11 touchdowns. This year in Philly, Wicks is projected to be a starter and will begin the season as the Eagles’ No. 2 receiver behind DeVonta Smith.

This is a big opportunity for Wicks. He worked as hard as possible to prepare for it. On Wednesday, Wicks was asked what Eagles fans can expect from him.

“A dawg that’s going to go out and give it my all,” Wicks said. “And put everything on the line for the guys around me. Like I said, just going out there and doing my 1/11 and trusting the people around me and just putting everything out there. That’s what you’re going to get from me. Trust that I’m going to go out there and give it my all even when things are going good or bad, I’m going to be out there. I love the game so I’m going to do what I do.”

The art of the spin move

During Thursday’s practice, we saw edge rusher Jalyx Hunt spending some extra time working on an inside spin move to add to his repertoire. And it looked pretty good.

Because veteran Arnold Ebiketie has been known for his spin move, we asked him what it takes to run an effective one. His biggest point was that you have to pick your moment.

“I think it’s a feel. It’s also about knowing when to use it,” Ebiketie explained. “The spin move is a tricky move. You can use it and it works or you can use it and it makes you look bad. You got to make sure the slide is not coming your way. It’s one of those things that I’ve used over the years. Usually, at the end of the game. It’s a good counter.”

Ebiketie said using the inside spin move is a great counter but once you run it once, the tackle is unlikely to overset again. So you’ve really got one shot at it.

Big Willie Style

Eagles offensive lineman Willie Lampkin has an unusual build at just 5-foot-11, but that gives him some unique potential as a special teams player.

The Eagles plan on utilizing his ability.

“Everybody’s not made the same, but you have different qualities that I’m able to use,” special teams coordinator Michael Clay said this week. “Jordan Davis and Jordan Mailata on field goal, that’s a pretty good edge to have right there. Vice versa with Willie, a guy that has that type of mobility, but still an offensive lineman, and he’s able to put his hands on somebody and drive them, that kind of creates a new running lane and a new idea. 

“I never want to put a player in a spot he doesn’t feel comfortable with because then he plays slow, then it’s all over the place. Once we have that rapport with Willie, which we have, and he feels confident, you can see that light turn off like, ‘Oh, this guy’s ready to go,’ we’re going to use anybody and everybody willing to help out this team [on] special teams.”

Advice from an Aussie 

The Rams and 49ers played the first-ever regular season NFL game in Australia on Thursday night. And they had very different travel plans. While the 49ers went about a week early to adjust to local time, the Rams tried to spend as little time as possible in Melbourne.

The 49ers won 27-7.

Eagles left tackle Jordan Mailata is an Australian native and has made the trip plenty of times. He said on Friday that he would have recommended going out early.

“Just because the flight itself is so long that I don’t think 24 hours is enough to flush out just that flight itself,” Mailata said. “It’s just not. You need a least a couple days. But, hey, what do I know? I’m not no sports scientist. I don’t know who came up with that but I just know I literally have a game plan for my flights when I got back home. You just have to.”

What is Mailata’s game plan? Pretty simple. Try to stay up when the flight begins until the first meal arrives and then for a few hours after eating. Then finally try to sleep for as long as you can. When you wake up, walk around the plane a bit. He has it down to a science.

And if the Eagles ever make that trip, maybe he’ll get a say in how they handle it.

Winning a job

It wasn’t much of a surprise this week when Vic Fangio finally named Marcus Epps the Eagles’ starting safety next to Drew Mukuba. All training camp, Epps appeared to be ahead of Michael Carter II. But Epps was gracious in victory this week.

“It was always close the whole time,” Epps said. “Mike Carter is a hell of a player, man. He can do a lot of different things on the field, play a lot of different positions. He’s real versatile. He’s just a really good ballplayer. I’m glad he’s on this team and I know he’s going to contribute to this team, to this defense this year as well.”

Epps said the competition “definitely” made him a better player this summer. At 30 years old, Epps is one of the Eagles’ oldest starters on the defensive side of the ball. He had to work his way through some “dark” times in rehab a couple years ago to get to this point.

“It feels good just to be back at this point and make it through what I’ve been through the last couple years,” Epps said. “But I’m focused on bigger and better things, man. Never trying to feel like I’m patting myself on the back or comfortable or complacent. Always working towards what’s next and how I can get better and help the team get better.”

A new banner

The Eagles had to take down all their banners outside the Linc for the World Cup this summer and one of those isn’t going back up. While those large banners to explicitly feature individual players, there was one that was obviously former Eagles receiver A.J. Brown.

Here’s what went up in its place this week on the west side of the stadium:

Week 1 success

The Eagles have been one of the best franchises in the NFL during Nick Sirianni’s five years at the helm. And they have gotten off to winning starts in all five season.

Since Sirianni took over in 2021, the Eagles are 5-0 in season openers. The only other team that’s undefeated in Week 1 in the same time frame is the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. And Sirianni is now tied with Greasy Neale (1942, 1944-47, excluding 1943 Steagles) for the Eagles’ longest streak of Week 1 victories.

When asked about Week 1 success, Sirianni unsurprisingly pointed at fundamentals.

“I’ve talked to a lot of different coaches and taken a lot of things from our examples of openers, and there’s a lot of common denominators,” Sirianni said. “Without getting too much into what they are, just for competitive reasons, there is no substitute for the work. There’s so many of those things that are key to Game 1, which we discussed as a team today, that you can’t cram for.”

item.title: Eagles vs. Commanders predictions for Week 1 of 2026 NFL season
item.description: Here are our predictions as the Eagles host the Commanders in Week 1 of the 2026 NFL season.
item.content:encoded:
Eagles vs. Commanders predictions for Week 1 of 2026 NFL season originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Eagles will kick off their 2026 season when they host the Washington Commanders at 4:25 p.m. on Sunday at the Linc.

Here are our predictions:

Reuben Frank (0-0)

Nobody has been better on opening day lately than the Eagles, who are undefeated in Week 1 under Nick Sirianni and an NFL-best 16-3 in openers since 2008. With a win against Washington, Jalen Hurts will become the first Eagles quarterback ever to win six openers. I expect an uneven performance from the offense Sunday with so much newness – new play caller, new scheme, new receivers – but this defense is so darn loaded I can’t picture the Commanders doing a lot of damage, even with a healthy Jayden Daniels. I feel like this game will be played in the high teens to low 20s with the defense dominating in the second half and the Eagles coming out on top for what would be a franchise-record-tying sixth straight opening-day win. Hurts is 8-1 against Washington with five straight wins in meaningful games when he plays the whole game. New offense or not, he’s not losing this one.

Eagles 23, Commanders 17

Dave Zangaro (0-0)

Even though some weird things seem to happen in Week 1, the Eagles are clearly the more talented team on Sunday. So I still think they’re going to win and it starts up front. On defense, the Eagles boast a talented defensive line that looks ready for a big season in 2026. Jalyx Hunt is coming off a tremendous training camp and he’ll be facing a backup left tackle in this game. He should get off to an incredibly quick start to his season. And then on the interior, Jalen Carter is healthy and in shape and is the centerpiece of what could be the best defense in the NFL. Even without Jonathan Greenard, I have faith in the defensive line.

On offense, the Eagles have a brand new scheme and while I generally think it will take some time to get this offense into a rhythm, they should be able to run the ball from the jump. Saquon Barkley has always killed the Commanders and that trend is going to continue on Sunday afternoon. I have him well over 100 yards and a touchdown as the Eagles cruise to a victory to start their 2026 season.

Eagles 27, Commanders 17

Barrett Brooks (0-0)

This offseason felt longer than usual. Let me start off with my prediction for the year: My Eagles will go 12-5 this year. They will win the division, even though they will split with the Cowboys.

Week 1 will be tough for the Birds because this is their first game in the new offense. I have very high expectations for Sean Manion. I really like this scheme for Jalen Hurts. I’m hoping he gets back to the run threat he was, threatening the defense and holding defenders in their gap disciplines. The game changer will be Saquon Barkley. I think he will run all over the Commanders’ defense for over 130 yards. Vic Fangio’s defense will be the other star in this game. Jayden Daniels will be sacked 4+ times and we will finally see the best trio of CBs in the league. The Birds win convincingly.

Eagles 28, Commanders 14  

Mike Mulhern (0-0)

Sunday’s matchup is full of unknowns. Two first-time play callers on offense for both teams. Sean Mannion and David Blough are young, up-and-coming former backup quarterbacks-turned offensive coordinators. Washington’s got a new defensive coordinator to boot in Daronte Jones. Figuring out what to expect in an era of no preseason reps and limited practice access is a bit of a fool’s errand. But early returns in Philadelphia are fairly positive for an offense in flux, while the Commanders experiment moving Jayden Daniels under center seems to be hitting even more speed bumps.

The Eagles’ defense is the one unit that hasn’t undergone wholesale changes. Even without Jonathan Greenard, they should have success up front against a depleted Commanders offensive line. Vic Fangio’s group is loaded and will surely have some surprises for Daniels, Blough, and company. Add in a heavy dose of Saquon Barkley and an electric crowd at the Linc and the Eagles once again walk away with a win in the season opener.

Eagles 28, Commanders 16

Ashlyn Sullivan (0-0)

The Eagles’ defensive line should be able to wreak havoc on a Commanders offensive line that was already weak but is now even weaker with the injury to their starting left tackle Laremy Tunsil. Brandon Coleman will go in for Tunsil at tackle and Eagles edge rusher Jalyx Hunt should have himself a day with this matchup. Week 1 is always a little weird and the Commanders have the element of surprise with a new offensive coordinator David Blough. I do expect the Eagles’ offense to look a bit clunky to start, but it will be enough to win this game against an opponent that has very little expectations in the division this year.

Eagles 24, Commanders 14 

Ryan Fowler (0-0)

Sunday is all about the trenches. On offense, while questions remain toward play sequencing from Sean Mannion and what the offense will actually look like in a live game setting, leaning on the front five and getting as many touches for Saquon Barkley should be the focus early against an underwhelming Commanders defensive front — despite the presence of Daron Payne and a faster, more athletic LB group headlined by top 10 pick Sonny Styles. Defensively, expect Washington to test Riq Woolen and Philly’s LBs in coverage with explosive TE Chig Okonkwo, but Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis should more than have their way against center Nick Allegretti and company, ultimately limiting space for Washington to execute. I’m also pumped to see Jalyx Hunt go to work. 

Overall, I expect a tight ballgame in Week 1. Washington touts one of football’s most dynamic young QBs in a prove-it year with talent present at the skill positions beyond Terry McLaurin, and a defense that, while underwhelming at corner, will fly around in DC Daronte Jones’ blitz-heavy scheme in an attempt to force turnovers. Washington has enough explosive talent to more than keep it competitive, but Philly’s ability to set the physical tone up front should wear down the Commanders over four quarters. 

Eagles 20, Commanders 17

item.title: Rutgers Second Half Push Comes Up Short in 28-21 Loss to Boston College
item.description: Rutgers falls to 0-2.
item.content:encoded:
After losing 37-21 in week one against UMass, Rutgers fell to a different team from Massachusetts in week 2 as they lost 28-21 to Boston College on the road. Despite a slight push in the second half, the Scarlet Knights couldn’t overcome a poor start and poor quarterback play to steal a win.

Rutgers found themselves in a steep hole early thanks to some turnovers, as they failed to score until they were down 17 points. The Knights would end the half down 20-7. Rutgers would rally to pull the game within a score a few times during the second half, but could not find a way to capitalize. After scoring in the third quarter to cut the deficit to 6, a blown coverage and a 78-yard touchdown pass and a following two-point conversion by the Eagles in the fourth quarter put Rutgers in a second two-touchdown hole that they could not climb out of despite having several opportunities to do so.

Quarterback AJ Surace had a rough first start in a Rutgers uniform, completing 18 out of 27 passes for three touchdowns and four interceptions. On the flip side, the Knights once again struggled to stop a mobile quarterback as Mason McKenzie completed 18 out of 29 passes for 252 yards, one touchdown and one interception while rushing for 94 yards and a touchdown on 13 carries.

Running back Antwan Raymond looked much better this game compared to last, totaling 134 yards on 27 carries, while backup running back Clay Thevenin ran for 36 yards on 7 carries. Their Boston College counterpart, Evan Dickens, recorded 56 yards and a touchdown on 13 carries.

Rutgers’ offensive line struggled to keep Surace upright, surrendering three sacks and five total tackles for loss throughout the game. The pressure on the defensive side of the ball for Rutgers wasn’t much better this game, only recording one sack and three tackles for loss.

The Knights offense failed to sustain drives throughout the game, going 4 of 12 on third down and 2 of 5 on fourth down while having 4 turnovers. Rutgers’ defense was more successful at getting off the field, holding Boston College to 4 of 12 on third down and causing 3 turnovers.

A bright spot for the Rutgers defense was linebacker Moses Walker, who recorded two interceptions, one sack, and four total tackles in the losing effort. On offense, KJ Duff once again proved why, despite questionable quarterback play, he is one of the best receivers in the country, recording eight catches for 137 yards and two touchdowns.

After dropping two games that most thought they would win at the beginning of the season, things will not get easier for the Knights from here on out, as they are set to open up Big Ten play next week at home against No. 14 USC. That is slated for a 3:30 p.m. kick on CBS.

item.title: Eagles send OC to booth, for first time under Nick Sirianni
item.description: In five years as the Eagles' head coach, Nick Sirianni has had his offensive coordinator on the field with him during the games.
item.content:encoded:
In five years as the Eagles' head coach, Nick Sirianni has had his offensive coordinator on the field with him during the games. For the first time in Sirianni's tenure, the man calling the plays on offense will be upstairs.

"We want to think through every situation to make sure that we're giving ourselves the best opportunity for us to win the game and be at our best," Sirianni told reporters on Friday regarding the decision to have Sean Mannion be in the booth. "Also understanding that there is no right way to do it or wrong way to do it. There's many different ways to do it. I think we can get caught up so much, it's like, 'This is the only way to do it.' You have conviction in what you believe, but there's many different things that can work and have worked. It's just about making the best decision, what's best for your football team and for you to do your job the best. That's how we went about it."

Sirianni was then asked how it will affect him to not have the offensive coordinator by his side during games.

"I don't think at all," Sirianni said. "I mean, obviously, there's communication still, right? We're talking on the headset and everything like that. I would say it's the amount of conversations that happen that have to be face-to-face, I think, are very minimal. I don't think that's -- you're being able to communicate and that's something that we stress on our players of how important communication is. We have to lead that as coaches as well. I don't think that affects us at all."

The balance continues to be seeing the full field for every play and having the ability to talk directly to the players without using a phone. And there is no magic to it. Nevertheless, it will be a different game-day experience for Sirianni, and for players like quarterback Jalen Hurts.

The first test of the new approach comes on Sunday, when the Eagles host the Commanders.

item.title: Ravens-Colts Week 1 predictions: how will Jesse Minter attack Daniel Jones?
item.description: The Ravens-Colts matchup should feature classic run-heavy, play-action offense from both sides.
item.content:encoded:
Let’s face it: odds probably do not mean much to Ravens fans at this point. Last year, Baltimore entered 14 games as favorites and won just half of them.

That pattern is likely to play out once again this year given the Ravens’ early slate of opponents, starting with the Colts in Week 1. Baltimore is favored by 3.5 points heading into Indianapolis (via FanDuel Sportsbook), indicating plenty of confidence in Jesse Minter’s head coaching debut.

The Colts are largely running it back with their 2025 squad, so last year’s tendencies can offer some insights into their plans for Sunday. Head coach Shane Steichen’s offense primarily operates out of the shotgun, relying on running back Jonathan Taylor to churn yards in the run game and suck linebackers in for play action shots to the intermediate areas of the field. Quarterback Daniel Jones rarely pushed the ball downfield, throwing deep balls less than 10% of the time (via Pro Football Focus). Most of those targets went to wide receiver Alec Pierce, the NFL’s back-to-back leader in yards per reception; beyond him, Indianapolis lacks another deep threat.

That should lead the Ravens to deploy some bracket coverage against Pierce to prevent him from taking the top off the defense. Minter’s three-safety looks will also allow the secondary to shift the coverage picture post-snap. Look out for Baltimore to bait Jones by showing a 1-on-1 matchup against Pierce pre-snap only for Malaki Starks or Jaylinn Hawkins to fly back and cover a potential shot downfield. If Indianapolis tries a high-low route combination on the outside, the boundary corner can try to jump the underneath route with safety help overtop.

The Colts’ defensive coordinator is a familar foe: Lou Anarumo, who previously held the same position in Cincinnati from 2019 to 2024. The Ravens offense largely found success against his Bengals defenses during his tenure, able to control games on the ground and keep up with Joe Burrow in a shootout when needed. But Anarumo’s ability to disguise his coverages and pressure packages can attack the Ravens offense in two key ways.

First, it will demand Jackson to be on the same page with a revamped offensive line that features a brand-new interior trio, including center Jovaughn Gwyn making his first start. He will already have his hands full with Colts defensive tackles DeForest Buckner and Grover Stewart, but he also has to help Jackson read the defense and communicate adjustments to the rest of the line.

Jackson will also have to be careful not to fall into Anarumo’s coverage traps. New offensive coordinator Declan Doyle has worked to re-establish the Ravens’ quick passing game with an emphasis on Jackson’s footwork and timing as he goes through his progression. But just as Minter will try to bait-and-switch Jones, Anarumo will do the same against Jackson.

This could become a particularly interesting battle when the Ravens go under center, which has been another of Doyle’s early focal points. Baltimore will no doubt use running back Derrick Henry to set up play-action shots to wide receiver Zay Flowers on his signature deep dig routes. Anarumo can respond with a two-high safety look but sending one of them to buzz the middle of the field. But that will only be possible if his front can stop the Ravens’ ground game, putting pressure on undersized linebackers Jaylon Carlies and Akeem Davis-Gaither to step up and fit the run. Otherwise, the Colts will have to use their safeties in run support, which should give Flowers more room to operate over the middle.

Given that this is his first game in Doyle’s system – and his first game back at 100% after last year’s injuries – the two-time MVP could lean on his legs on Sunday as he gets settled in the offense. Some of his most dazzling extended plays came against Anarumo’s Bengals, partially because the coverage look forced him to hold onto the ball.

These are just a few elements of the schematic battle set to take place on Sunday. Steichen and Anarumo will offer a solid first challenge to the Ravens’ new-look coaching staff in a game that could come down to Baltimore’s star power advantage on both sides of the ball.

item.title: Richard Sherman on 49ers defeating Rams: ‘Kyle Shanahan has Sean McVay’s number’
item.description: Few believed the San Francisco 49ers would defeat the Super Bowl favorite Los Angeles Rams in Australia. But Richard Sherman always knew. “They were in the broadcast talking about ‘undefeated...
item.content:encoded:
Few believed the San Francisco 49ers would defeat the Super Bowl favorite Los Angeles Rams in Australia.

But Richard Sherman always knew.

“They were in the broadcast talking about ‘undefeated season’ and almost everybody picked them to win this game like it wasn’t gonna be close. And I told people, I don’t know, I don’t have the Rams winning this game because Kyle Shanahan has Sean McVay’s number,” Sherman said on his podcast.

“And Rams fans said, oh you’re just a hater. Do I look like a hater now? Who looks right? I’m right. Ball knower. I know ball.”

The Rams were considered Super Bowl favorites even before trading for reigning Defensive Player of the Year Myles Garrett and cornerback Trent McDuffie. But Aaron Donald’s return was the icing on the cake for the juggernaut Rams.

Or at least it seemed to be.

But on Thursday, the Rams looked sluggish. The squad didn’t appear to be the superteam everyone had thought they’d be.

Many were quick to point out the travel plans, which may have been the wrong choice for the Rams. But head coach Sean McVay immediately gave the 49ers credit for a commanding 27-7 win over LA.

“First of all, congratulations to the 49ers. They outplayed us in every facet,” Rams head coach Sean McVay said postgame.

“I didn’t do nearly a good enough job. This is a humbling day for us, and this will define us only if we allow it to. And today was one of those days. I always look inside out. I didn’t do a good enough job getting us ready to go.”

The Rams’ performance in Melbourne shouldn’t be a reason to panic just yet, but any hopes of an untarnished season have gone out the door. As for the 49ers, it appears their defense entered the 2026 season with question marks but put all doubts about the unit to rest against the Rams.

item.title: Odell Beckham Jr. returns to vintage Giants form — in more ways than just his hair
item.description: Odell Beckham Jr. couldn’t have paid one of his Hollywood friends to write a better script for the start of his Giants sequel.
item.content:encoded:
Odell Beckham Jr. couldn’t have paid one of his Hollywood friends to write a better script for the start of his Giants sequel. 

A Giants-Cowboys game on Sunday Night Football at MetLife Stadium — the stage that made him internationally famous because of his one-handed catch as a rookie in 2014 — feels to him like proof of his belief in a higher power’s mysterious ways. 

Access the Giants like never before

Get texts from Paul Schwartz with all the latest Giants news and insights, exclusive to Sports+ subscribers.

tRY IT NOW

“I always talk about God’s plan,” Beckham said after Friday’s practice. “Right when I was [trying out] and I was seeing all these things happening, the NFL was like, ‘Giants, Sunday night, Cowboys.’ It’s just crazy because everything that’s happened with that. You just try to be in the moment and not overthink.” 

But Beckham, 33, fed into the throwback storyline by dyeing his hair platinum blond — his signature color — after wearing it black all summer. He kept a helmet and hat on when cameras were around this week to keep the look secret for the Sunday audience. 

“I kind of got a request from a couple of the young guys, like, ‘We need to see the blond. I need that as a core memory,’” Beckham said. “It’s always fun to switch it up. I can have black hair forever. I can’t fry this forever, and it might grow back. Now was the time.” 

Beckham had all the time in the world ahead of him on Nov. 23, 2014, when he reached over his head while drawing pass interference, grabbed Eli Manning’s pass with three fingers and fell backward into the end zone for a touchdown. The Giants’ loss that night became a postscript. 

The result Sunday — in John Harbaugh’s first game as head coach — is not meaningless. 

“They asked me, like, ‘Are you going to recreate it on Sunday?’” Beckham said. “I’m like, ‘Bro, I didn’t try to do it.’ It just came with the preparation and the practice. I’m like, ‘I’ve dropped a lot of one-hands, too.’ But it changed my life forever … for better or for worse, because people try and amount the whole career into one play.” 

One-handed catches instantly became part of football practices from Pop Warner to the NFL. The catch’s degree of difficulty has been matched but Beckham’s is most memorable. 

“I have four boys and one of them is a receiver at Kansas right now,” Giants offensive coordinator Matt Nagy said. “And I know for the past, like, six years in the offseason, they’re always trying in the offseason to do one-hand catches. 

“I got to see Odell when he was in his prime then and just had a ton of respect for him. And to see him now with where he’s at in this part of the career, I think you really start to appreciate where you’re at and now it’s the team part and he’s embraced that.” 

After looking washed up with the 2024 Dolphins and sitting out all of 2025, a healthy Beckham beat the odds by making the Giants’ 53-man roster in training camp. He is one of only four receivers, so he should see snaps. 

Sunday will be his first regular-season game with the Giants in 2,842 days — since Week 13 of 2018. In that game, the electric Beckham Version 1.0 caught a touchdown, threw a touchdown and misplayed an onside kick. 

Former teammates have texted Beckham to remind him that he is playing for another era. 

“They always talk about, ‘We’re living through you,’” Beckham said. “I see guys who I played here with and they’re like, ‘It’s just crazy. It’s a tremendous amount of top off to you and the work that you did to get back here.’ But not too many people get a chance to have this kind of story written up, and I just want to take advantage of that.” 

If the preseason is any indication, Beckham will do his traditional one-handed catch end-zone warm-up before the game, and the home crowd will cheer his every move. 

“If I get that opportunity to run out and I could hear this stadium, which I feel like is just going to erupt, I think that’ll be the moment where your chest tightens up a little bit and eyes might get a little watery,” Beckham said. 

“I just love this game and I’ve sacrificed my whole life for it. And I just want to give this city, this organization, these fans, every last bit of me. Whatever that is, I came to give it.”

item.title: Texans Place Rookie DT Kayden McDonald on IR
item.description: The rookie second-round pick will miss at least the first four games after suffering an ankle injury during practice.
item.content:encoded:
On the eve of their regular season debut, the Houston Texans have announced another significant injury. Rookie DT Kayden McDonald is apparently suffering from an ankle injury and will begin the regular season on injured reserve. Battle Red Blog’s Nickschwager noted McDonald’s appearance on the injury report yesterday, but a placement on IR is a new and rather sudden development.

McDonald will now be inactive for the first four games of the 2026 regular season: vs. Buffalo Bills, vs. Cincinnati Bengals, @ Indianapolis Colts, and vs. Dallas Cowboys. He will be eligible to return for Houston’s match against the Tennessee Titans on October 11th. In the meantime, the Texans are signing DT Jaden Crumedy from the Green Bay Packers practice squad.

Houston Chronicle reporter Jonathan M. Alexanderstated following the announcement, “McDonald suffered the injury in practice Wednesday, a league source said. He did not practice Thursday or Friday and wore a protective boot over his foot in the locker room”

Kayden McDonald, despite being a rookie second-round pick, was fixing to have a significant impact on Houston’s dominant defensive line. He earned first team All-American honors while starting for Ohio State in 2025, and quickly ascended draft boards after establishing himself as one of the best run-stoppers in the 2026 NFL Draft. He had a lot of fans here at Battle Red Blog, and I even got the chance to ask him a question representing the Blog at the 2026 NFL Draft in Pittsburgh:

He finished his final collegiate season with 65(!) tackles, a preposterous stat for a beefy interior lineman, and his pass-rush seemed to be improving down the stretch. Fortunately for the Texans, they still have depth in the interior defensive line, with starting DTs Sheldon Rankins and Tommy Togiai still expected to absorb the majority of snaps. But, McDonald was brought in with the express purpose of being a run-stuffer who would contribute on early downs, something that could have pushed this defense to even greater heights. And, don’t look now, but there are currently four Texans defensive linemen on IR: McDonald, DE Dylan Horton, DE Solomon Byrd, and DE Ali Gaye. Fortunately, none of these players are starters, but depth at a pretty important spot on this year’s Texans team is now significantly thinner, especially during a fairly grizzly opening slate of games. We already know the Cowboys and Bills have great offenses, but the Bengals and Colts could both find themselves near to the top of the league in offensive production by year’s end, too. 

Regardless, this Texans defense is one of the few groups in the league that can push through this wave of injuries relatively unscathed. Togiai, Mario Edwards Jr. and free-agent addition DT Logan Hall will have bigger roles this Sunday trying to contain defending NFL rushing leader RB James Cook, who ran for 116 yards and a touchdown at a piercing 6.8 Y/A against our mighty Texans defense in Week 12 last year. They’re hands will be very, very full this coming Sunday, but if there was a team able to take this blow and keep charging forward, it’s this Texans team!

What do you think of this news? Are the Texans in more danger of losing their first game of the season because of this injury, or was McDonald just going to play a small role? Will new DT Jaden Crumedy surprise us all and make some sweet tackles in Week 1, or will Logan Hall have a banner game to start his Texans tenure? Let us know your thoughts down in the comments below!

Go Texans!

item.title: Rams’ disastrous performance against 49ers featured one jarring surprise, says analyst
item.description: The Los Angeles Rams didn't look like a Super Bowl contender in their season opener.
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Rams didn’t look like a Super Bowl contender in their season opener.

The Rams, who were dubbed as the favorites to hoist the Lombardi Trophy at the end of the season, looked mediocre in Week 1 against the San Francisco 49ers.

Head coach Sean McVay was out-coached. Quarterback Matthew Stafford played poorly. Reigning Defensive Player of the Year Myles Garrett was nowhere to be found, recording zeros across the board in his Rams debut.

And Aaron Donald was watching the Australia showdown from LA.

The result? The 49ers handed the Super Bowl favorites a 27-7 beatdown in their season opener.

NFL analyst Danny Parkins shared what surprised him the most about the Rams’ lackluster performance Thursday.

“I think the most surprising thing about the whole thing is seven points. The Rams scored seven points in a football game,” Parkins said on First Things First.

“I just could not stop thinking about the ineptitude of the Rams offense.”

It was the Rams’ largest loss in 38 games. It was the fewest points scored in a Stafford start in 84 games. Stafford posted the lowest passer rating he’s had in 70 games and it was the first time in 18 games that he recorded zero touchdowns.

The notion that Week 1 lies remains true, but the Rams certainly didn’t set the tone for what was poised to be an electric season with their disappointing performance in Melbourne.

item.title: Bills' initial grass field had "major deformations"
item.description: In six days, the Bills will host the first regular-season game at their new stadium.
item.content:encoded:
In six days, the Bills will host the first regular-season game at their new stadium. On the second new field there.

The team decided to replace the grass after only two preseason games.

Via Tim Graham of The Athletic, NFL field expert Nick Pappas explained what went wrong with the first field installed there.

"The aspect of the field that appeared to be an issue was that there were major deformations happening, large divoting outside of what we typically see at many of our NFL grass fields — although not something we haven’t seen before," Pappas told Graham. "That lent itself to say there was an opportunity to improve that surface, and that’s what the Bills have stepped up to do and made that decision to replace it."

Pappas explained that, whenever a new stadium is built, "There’s a period before it gets turned over to Bills staff. So, you’re now reliant on the general contractor or the installation company for maintenance over a certain period of time."

He attributed the situation to a "combination of the sod quality from the start, the challenges, and maybe the management up until the Bills’ grounds crew were able to take over, and then you couple it with a very new growing environment that needs to be worked through."

Pappas said the new sod "will come in thicker" than the prior version.

The next challenge becomes preparing the field for three home games in three weeks: Week 2, Week 3, and Week 4.

Pappas thinks another replacement will likely happen during the season.

"Recovery needs to outpace usage," he said. "But if the weather is great and all goes well over that three-game stand, maybe they’re looking at Week 8 to replace it, or they can look at the weather and say, 'Hey, based on where we are today, we have three weeks to recover. We can bring the grow lights out. We can provide our agronomic program with fertility and grow it back.'"

Given the weather challenges in Buffalo, Pappas said he wouldn't be surprised if the Bills need three or four fields per year.

That's one of the reasons why some teams prefer artificial turf. It's cheaper. It doesn't require constant evaluation.

But if teams and owners care about giving their players the surface they prefer, it's worth the money and the effort. Despite the challenges the Bills are facing, they deserve credit for trying to give the players the best possible surface.

item.title: NFL Week 1 Bears-Panthers Predictions: Which run defense will step up?
item.description: This feels like a lot of ground-and-pound upcoming for the Bears and Panthers. @BryanOrenchuk explores it here.
item.content:encoded:
The Carolina Panthers have not won a Week 1 game since 2021, but they are coming off a playoff season in 2025. Could they beat the Chicago Bears outright at home or at least cover the spread?

Much has been made of the trade that brought Caleb Williams to Chicago and Bryce Young to Carolina. Since the two QBs have taken over for their respective squads, the Bears have gone 16-18 (11-6 under Ben Johnson), and the Panthers have gone 15-36.

Both teams are coming off strong seasons with playoff appearances led by their run games, and both teams made substantial acquisitions this offseason, especially on defense. Chicago signed S Coby Bryant and LB Devin Bush while Carolina added LB Devin Lloyd and Edge Jaelan Phillips. Obviously, Chicago fans know Bryant will miss most of the year with an injury, but the question remains for both teams.

Can they slow down their opponent’s offense this week?

For a Chicago defense that allowed the 6th most rushing yards a season ago, the Panthers know they have to establish the run and build off their 2025 season, when they ranked in the top 20 in both rushing yards and attempts per game. Chicago will be leaning heavily on a couple rookies, Jordan van den Berg and Jayden Loving, and 9th-year pro Kentavius Street, whom Bears DC Dennis Allen said had the strongest camp of any DT on the roster.

For the Panthers, the addition of Lloyd and Phillips will most certainly help, but the Panthers defense still relies on the play of All-World DT Derrick Brown to slow down opposing offenses. Especially the run game. That said, the edge for best DL seems to go to Carolina in this one. However, in his first 3 career Week 1 starts, Bryce Young has thrown a combined 2 TDs and 6 INTs and has yet to throw for more than 200 yards. Which leads even more credence to the idea that the Panthers should “Keep Pounding” the ball on the ground this week.

Our friends at FanDuel Sportsbook currently have the Bears as 3-point favorites for this week’s contest in Carolina. If you think the Bears will win outright, the moneyline is at -176, with the point total over/under at 47.5.

I am predicting a 31-20 Bears win, with both D’Andre Swift and Chuba Hubbard to lead their teams with over 70 yards rushing each – and that’ll hit the over on their betting lines in this one, with Swift currently at 63.5 and Hubbard at 50.5.
