item.title: ESPN analyst sounds alarm on Rams defensive coordinator: ‘They have stunk’
item.description: A small sample can still contain a large warning. Dan Orlovsky found one in Melbourne, where the Rams’ celebrated defense looked considerably less imposing than the collection of names Los...
item.content:encoded:
A small sample can still contain a large warning.

Dan Orlovsky found one in Melbourne, where the Rams’ celebrated defense looked considerably less imposing than the collection of names Los Angeles assembled during the offseason.

After initially criticizing Matthew Stafford’s performance in the Rams’ 27-7 loss to the 49ers, Orlovsky redirected the spotlight toward defensive coordinator Chris Shula.

“This ain’t the flaw, and this is not the concern,” Orlovsky said on ESPN’s “Get Up!” “I am very concerned about that defense, and I’m very concerned about their defensive coordinator.”

Orlovsky extended his argument beyond Week 1.

“The last four games that we have watched this defense on the field with all kinds of talent, they have stunk,” he said. “Bryce Young lit them up. Caleb Williams lit them up. Sam Darnold lit them up. Brock Purdy lit them up.”

The early schematic numbers make Orlovsky’s criticism more interesting.

During the 2025 regular season, the Rams ran defensive-line stunts on approximately 41.7% of opposing dropbacks. That rate fell to 19.4% against San Francisco. Their use of schemed pressures — a broader category incorporating blitzes, simulated pressures and other nontraditional rushes — dropped from 39.1% to 25%.

Traditional blitz frequency also declined from approximately 18% to 14%.

It is only 36 dropbacks against one opponent, making any conclusion provisional. San Francisco’s quick passing game also reduced the time available for pressures to reach Purdy.

Still, it is fair to wonder whether the Rams ended up oversimplifying their rush plan while integrating Myles Garrett, believing the reigning Defensive Player of the Year could consistently win without schematic assistance. Perhaps fewer stunts and simulated pressures were installed because Shula expected his four-man rush to create disruption without them.

There is no evidence establishing that as Shula’s thinking. If it was the bet, however, it failed spectacularly. The Rams did not sack Purdy, while Garrett finished without a tackle or quarterback hit.

The coverage choices created another contradiction.

Cover 3 and Cover 2 were the Rams’ most frequently used coverages in 2025, accounting for approximately 33% and 19% of dropbacks. Against San Francisco, Cover 3 and Cover 4 each appeared on roughly 31%, while Cover 2 disappeared from the small sample.

The Rams’ man-coverage rate simultaneously fell from approximately 20% to 14%.

Cover 4 frequently incorporates pattern-matching principles that resemble man coverage, so the shift cannot be reduced to Shula simply calling passive zone. But playing less conventional man is curious after Los Angeles paid heavily to acquire Trent McDuffie, one of the NFL’s premier man-coverage cornerbacks. His arrival was supposed to expand Shula’s menu, including the aggressive pressure packages made possible when a corner can survive without help.

Personnel usage produced a similar question. Nickel increased from roughly 42% to 47%, but dime fell from approximately 32% to 25% despite a secondary featuring McDuffie, Jaylen Watson, Kamren Curl, Quentin Lake and Kamren Kinchens.

San Francisco’s heavy personnel and productive running game offered a logical reason to keep additional size on the field. Still, Curl and Lake are precisely the hybrid defenders who should allow the Rams to play dime without becoming defenseless against the run.

That makes Curl’s ankle injury especially meaningful. His ability to operate in the box, cover from the slot, play deep and join pressure packages connects multiple sections of Shula’s defense. If he misses more time, a dime package already used less frequently becomes harder to disguise and deploy.

One game is not enough to declare that the Rams have changed their defensive identity. Aaron Donald has yet to return, Garrett was playing through a knee issue and each opponent demands a different plan.

The concern is that Shula’s opening plan deemphasized several tools this roster was specifically constructed to exploit.

The Rams have more than enough defensive talent. Orlovsky is questioning whether their coordinator is making opposing quarterbacks account for all of it.

item.title: Packers release WR Bo Melton, intend to retain him on practice squad
item.description: Melton’s release appears to be procedural to open up a roster spot, but the mechanics remain a bit unclear.
item.content:encoded:
Just over 48 hours ahead of their season opener, the Green Bay Packers have made a mildly shocking roster move. According to Adam Schefter of ESPN, the Packers are releasing wide receiver Bo Melton on Friday.

Melton has been a mainstay of the Packers’ special teams units for the past two-plus years and has remained a valuable depth piece in the wide receiver room, even despite being his supposed position switch to cornerback for the 2025 season. As one of the team’s primary punt gunners and kickoff coverage players, Melton logged over 300 special teams snaps across the last two seasons, and the team’s coverage units visibly suffered late in 2025 when he missed the last few games with an injury.

Packers beat reporters all reported that the move is related to roster management and that the Packers expect Melton to remain in the organization on the practice squad in week one.

There is some question about whether Melton can immediately re-sign with the Packers, however. Melton appears to have only three accrued seasons of NFL experience (defined as 6 or more games on full-pay status). That woould not qualify him for vested veteran status and would require that he clear waivers before the Packers can re-sign him to the practice squad. Should another NFL team claim him, the Packers would lose Melton entirely. With Melton currently on a league-minimum contract, he could feasibly be an intriguing target for other teams around the NFL, especially one that, for example, has a general manager, head coach, and quarterback who are familiar with him from their time in Green Bay over the last few years. Frankly, it would be a coup for the Miami Dolphins if they were to land Melton for free given their young and inexperienced stable of receivers and Melton’s familiarity with Malik Willis.

Tom Silverstein, however, indicates that Melton is a vested veteran and therefore immediately becomes a free agent, which would allow him to immediately re-sign with the Packers’ practice squad.

The Packers signed Melton away from the Seattle Seahawks’ practice squad late in the 2022 season, and he then spent most of the 2023 campaign on the Packers’ practice squad. However, he earned a callup to the active roster in November and exploded onto the scene with a 6-catch, 105-yard, game against the Minnesota Vikings on New Year’s Eve. That was the Packers’ first 100-yard receiving game by any player that season, and he continued his breakout a week late with another 62 yards on five receptions in the season finale while being on full-pay status for six games, thereby earning an accrued season for 2023.

Melton then spent 2024 buried on the wide receiver depth chart as the team’s 5th/6th wideout, only catching 8 passes despite playing in every game and logging 251 offensive snaps, but he made a name for himself on the special teams units. Melton remained an option for the offense in 2025 after his formal switch to cornerback, and he still recorded 4 receptions for 107 yards, including a long touchdown in the Packers’ week 13 win over the Bears, while never actually taking a snap on defense.

If Melton is indeed vested, then this makes some sense, but it still requires explanation. Why do the Packers need the roster spot? The team clearly is making space for some corresponding move, though that move has not yet been reported.

Stay tuned for news that will hopefully explain why this move is happening, and why now is the time for it.

UPDATE: Matt Schneidman further reports that Melton is, somehow, a vested veteran, and that there is no corresponding move to fill his spot on the 53-man roster.

UPDATE:From APC’s own Justis Mosqueda in the comments section.

Alright, here’s the info I have at this point:

Wendell Ferreira’s information that Bo Melton was credited for four seasons (this changed this offseason; he was previously listed with three by the NFLPA) is true.

Basically, there are two ways the NFL counts NFL tenure: accrued seasons and credited seasons.

Accrued seasons means that you’re on the NFL’s active/inactive lists (including healthy scratches and scratches for injuries) for at least six weeks of a regular season. This impacts things like the exclusive rights/restricted free agent tenders a player can receive. Melton has two of these accrued seasons, as he only played in five games for the 2023 Packers and wasn’t on the field at all for his rookie season of 2022. This is why he’s four years into his NFL career but was only hit with the exclusive rights free-agent tender (typical for free agents coming out of their second season in the league).

A credited season is when a player has been on the active/inactive roster for at least three games. This impacts things like whether a player is counted as a vested veteran for the waiver process or veteran termination pay. Melton has four of these because his 2022 season with the Packers (he was on the team for just two weeks) counted as a three-week stay. The reason for this is that players poached from practice squads (as Melton was from Seattle) receive a guaranteed three weeks’ worth of pay. So he was paid for three weeks, even though the Packers only had two weeks left in the regular season and missed the playoffs.

Again, there was some debate about Melton’s credited seasons at one point this offseason, as the timing of his 2022 addition put him in a unique spot. It’s not often that a rookie Week 16 practice squad elevation in a non-playoff year plays between 2 and 5 games in his second year with the team and ends up making the roster three years down the line, putting this rule of a two-year accrued player and four-year credited player in play.

Because Melton is credited with four seasons, Melton was allowed to be released by the Packers without subjecting him to waivers, which is why he was quickly picked up on the practice squad (Green Bay had a vacancy because defensive tackle Jaden Crumedy was claimed by the Houston Texans today).

Veteran termination pay (what people usually refer to as a veteran’s salary becoming guaranteed in Week 1) is based on credited seasons, which is almost certainly why the Packers made this move (on top of the practice squad vacancy). Moving forward, Green Bay will be able to release Melton from their 53-man roster (once he’s added back up) without penalty, whereas if they kept him on the 53-man roster, they would have been down about a million dollars minimum (assuming Melton filed for the once-in-career opportunity for termination pay).

Thank you for reading about this hyper-niche roster move that will ultimately mean nothing when Melton plays on Sunday and is added back to the 53-man roster in the near future. It bothered me enough that I pestered people in the league about it on a Friday.

item.title: Las Vegas Raiders-Miami Dolphins FEED topic: How much has offensive line improved?
item.description: What we’re focusing on in The FEED for this week’s game.
item.content:encoded:
Silver and Black Pride is bringing back the game-day discussions on The FEED this season, where we’ll focus on and talk about a specific topic for each Las Vegas Raiders game. This won’t replace our open thread on game days, which is designed to focus on the game as a whole.

For the Raiders’ Week 1 matchup against the Miami Dolphins, we’ll be paying close attention to how much Las Vegas’ offensive line has actually improved from last year.

It’s no secret that the Raiders’ offensive line was downright putrid during the 2025 season. Hence why the front office made Tyler Linderbaum the highest-paid center in NFL history by $9 million per year, and why head coach Klint Kubiak brought over long-time offensive line coach Rich Dennison this offseason. The Silver and Black will also get Kolton Miller back after Miller missed 13 out of 17 games with an ankle injury a year ago.

All of that, plus a solid showing in the preseason, gives reason for optimism when it comes to the trenches in Las Vegas. However, now it’s time to prove it by getting results on the field when the competition level rises and the games actually count. And there are still plenty of question marks within the unit.

Free-agent signing Spencer Burford was never challenged for the starting left guard spot despite struggling to stick as a starter during his last two seasons with the San Francisco 49ers. Burford likely knows Kubiak’s offense better than anyone else on the line, having worked with Kubiak in San Francisco for a year (2023) and playing in a similar system under 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan. But is that enough to justify a starting spot, and has the fifth-year pro turned the corner?

Meanwhile, 2024 draftees Jackson Powers-Johnson and DJ Glaze are slated to man the right guard and right tackle spots, respectively. Both players have shown flashes, primarily during their rookie campaigns, but have struggled to be consistent so far.

Powers-Johnson even had to fend off Caleb Rogers to keep his spot in the starting lineup. There was a moment when it seemed rookie Trey Zuhn III might push Glaze, but the latter took most, if not all, of the first-team reps at right tackle during training camp. So, it’s certainly worth keeping tabs on the right side of the line to see how the third-year pros look.

Granted, the Dolphins don’t have many defensive linemen who should keep opposing offenses up at night. Like the Raiders, they hit the reset button in the offseason and moved on several notable players. Edge rusher Bradley Chubb led Miami with 8.5 sacks in 2025, three more than anyone else, but the 30-year-old was a salary cap casualty. However, that creates an opportunity for 2024 first-round pick Chop Robinson to take on a bigger role.

Robinson battled injuries and regressed last season with just four sacks, but he had six sacks and was one of the best rookie pass-rushers just two years ago. The Penn State product is known for his speed and athleticism on the edge, which has been one of Glaze’s issues.

In the running game and on the interior, Burford and Powers-Johnson will be tested by Miami’s defensive tackle Zach Sieler. The nine-year pro doesn’t get a ton of attention in the media, but he’s posted double-digit TFLs in each of the last three seasons and four out of the last six. Also, Sieler is coming off a down year as a pass rusher, but he’s been plenty productive in that department, too. Having Linderbaum at center can help stabilize the interior offensive line, but the guards also have to hold up their end of the bargain.

So, we’ll be focusing on how the Raiders’ offensive line performs against the Dolphins in this week’s game day discussion over on The FEED. The game kicks off at 1:25 p.m. PST and will air on FOX (check your local listings). I look forward to talkin’ some ball with y’all!

item.content:encoded:
A funny comment from Courtland Sutton surfaced this week when he called Bo Nix a mountain lion. Nix was asked about it and had to think a bit before coming to the conclusion that he liked the comparison.

“I think out here there are different animals that you can encounter,” Nix said. “I hear a lot of the times it’s mountain lions and bears that you don’t want to come across. I guess that is a good comparison and one that I will take. I definitely think the thing about mountain lions is usually that when you notice them, it’s because they noticed you a long time ago. I’m just excited to get out there. I feel like I’m pacing and feel like I’ve been in this practice schedule for a long time. It’s exciting to go out there and play another team. It’s really exciting and I know that our guys are going to respond well. I feel like I have a great group with me that I’m going in here with. I can’t wait.”

A mountain lion is a pure hunter and as a quarterback sometimes you have to hunt and in NFL terms that would be putting a dagger in the team trying to make a comeback or mounting your own comeback to help the team win the game. Bo has done a lot of the latter and I hope to see some of the former this year.

item.title: Kansas State Football: Washington State Preview – Offense
item.description: Washington State needs to run the ball. There are some questions about K-State’s ability to stop the run. Those questions will be answered, one way or another, on Saturday.
item.content:encoded:
Quarterback

Caden Pinnick – 6’0”, 192 – 3rd Year Player – UC Davis

Week 1 vs Washington: 16/25, 142 Yds, 0 Tds, 2 Int, 14 Rushes, 61 Yds, 1 Td

Thoughts:

That stat line pretty much says it all. Pinnick isn’t so much a dual-threat quarterback as he is a single-threat quarterback, with that threat being his legs. He reminds me a little of former Wildcat quarterback Alex Delton. Physically, he can throw the ball, but his decision-making makes it a risky proposition. Of the 25 passes he attempted against Washington, only 5 went over 10 yards in the air. Interestingly enough, he completed all 5 of those passes (4 to his team and 1 to Washington).

The game plan against these types of quarterbacks isn’t hard to conceptualize, but the execution of said game plan can be an entirely different story. The defensive line has to be patient, stay in their rush lanes, and collapse the pocket around Pinnick. Kansas State needs to force him to step up in the pocket and into the lap of the waiting defensive tackles. The worst thing you can do is have a defensive end come off the edge hot, looking for a sack, and come up empty, letting him get to the perimeter where his legs become a problem. This isn’t a guy the defense should be chasing; he’s a guy they should be containing and encouraging to throw the football.

I don’t think Pinnick can beat Kansas State with his arm from the pocket. There’s a chance he can beat them by making plays in the open field. Patience will be a virtue for the Wildcat edge rushers on Saturday.

Running Back

Leo Pulalasi – 6’1”, 208 – 4th Year Player – Washington State

Week 1 vs Washington: 5 Rushes, 13 Yards, 3 Rec, 12 Yds

and

Kirby Vorhees – 5’11”, 215 – 4th Year Player – South Dakota State

Week 1 vs Washington: 7 Rushes, 17 Yards, 2 Rec, 13 Yds

Thoughts:

With Pinnick at quarterback, this team is all-in on running the ball; unfortunately, they weren’t particularly effective at it against Washington’s physical defensive front, despite starting two tailbacks and a running quarterback. All of Pulalasi’s attempts were A- and B-gap runs last week. He’s a big, strong back, but he never had a chance to get his long legs churning in the opener.

At 5’11”, 215, Vorhees is a compact ball of muscle. Like Pulalasi, he’s looking to run straight ahead as opposed to outflanking the defense; that’s Pinnick’s job. Washington State wants to use their running backs as sledgehammers to soften up the defensive front and push safeties and linebackers inside, so their quarterback can pull the ball and get outside. Washington didn’t allow them any success in the A gaps, and that’s going to be the task for Kansas State’s front 6 (or 7) tomorrow.

Wide Receiver

Darius Clemons – 6’3”, 217 – 4th Year Player – UMich/Oregon St.

Week 1 vs Washington: 3 Rec, 40 Yds

Daniel Blood – 5’11”, 190 – 4th Year Player – Missouri

Week 1 vs Washington: 5 Rec, 57 Yds

Thoughts:

Another reason I expect the Cougs to lean heavily on the run game is the week-one knee injury to their dynamic slot receiver, Tony Freeman. It sounds like Freeman isn’t going to be able to go, leaving Clemons and Blood to pick up the slack. Out of the two, Blood looked more dangerous against the Huskies, including hauling in a game-high 32-yard reception down the right sideline. It’s possible Blood was open deep because the defense expected him to be closer to the line of scrimmage. For the most part, he’s responsible for the short and intermediate routes in this offense, which also happens to be where Pinnick wants to throw the ball.

Clemons did most of his work against Washington in the 10–20-yard range. He’s a physical receiver who doesn’t mind going over the middle and taking a hit to make a catch, but is more of a “catch it and get down” receiver as opposed to a “catch it and run” receiver. My only concern is Clemons using his strength to break an initial tackle and then finding room to run. Washington did a good job playing tight coverage and getting him to the ground on the initial tackle attempt. It would serve the Wildcats well to do the same.

Tight End

Jack Pederson – 6’5”, 250 – 5th Year Player – UCLA

Week 1 vs Washington: 1 Rec, 3 Yds

With Freeman going to an injury in the first quarter, Pederson found himself on the field for 54 snaps. He’s a de facto offensive lineman in this offense and is much more likely to make an impact in the run game as a blocker than in the passing game as a receiver.

Offensive Line

Left Tackle

Ashton Tripp – 6’7”, 307 – 4th Year Player – Washington State

Left Guard

Kyle Martin – 6’3”, 310 – 2nd Year Player – Washington State

Center

Noah Dunham – 6’5”, 292 – 3rd Year Player – Washington State

Right Guard

Nick Bakken – 6’5”, 305 – 2nd Year Player – South Dakota State

Right Tackle

Jonny Lester – 6’5”, 320 – 3rd Year Player – Washington State

Thoughts:

I thought this would be Washington State’s strength heading into the season, but that didn’t play out in the opener. As I mentioned earlier, the Huskies are stout up front, and the Cougar offensive line couldn’t push them off the line enough to give their running backs a chance to get started. This offense is built to run the football, but that can’t happen if there’s no place to run but into the arms of a waiting defender. I don’t think they have any option but to line up again this week, try what didn’t work in week 1 again, and hope for better results.

If I’m Cougar offensive coordinator Matt Miller, I’m looking at the middle of the Wildcats defensive line and feeling better about my chances of getting the interior run game going. We’ll find out tomorrow if the Kamari Burns and Travis Bates pairing can hold up against a team that makes a concerted effort to run in the A-gaps. This should be an interesting stress test for a position group, and I wouldn’t be surprised to see more from Eli Jackson and De’Arieun Hicks in this game as Coach Peterson tries to keep his interior line from wearing down. I could also see 1st-year defensive tackle Carnell Jackson Jr. get some run as the only true nose tackle on the team. I’m not sure he’s ready yet, but he’s also 6’2, 350 pounds, and that could come in handy against a team that needs to run inside.

One potential issue for Kansas State is the health of middle linebacker Meki Mason. If Mason can’t go, Rex Van Wyhe is going to need to step up to help shut down the interior run game. In my humble opinion, playing a 4-3-3 makes more sense against a run-dependent offense like Washington State, but I’m not sure that’s an option for this defense without Mason on the field. Keep an eye on safety Logan Bartley; he may be playing a little closer to the line of scrimmage than usual tomorrow, and while I love Koy Beasley’s speed on the back end, Adrian Maddox could get some additional run as the more physical safety.

Overall

Washington State couldn’t get anything going on offense in the Apple Cup last week. The Huskies shut down the interior run, kept Pinnick from doing too much damage with his legs, and forced him to try and win the game from the pocket.

That seems like a winning game plan this week, too. Everything hinges on stopping the inside run.

If Washington State gets it going between the tackles, Pinnick’s ability to pull the ball and attack the edges is significantly more dangerous because the defensive ends will be looking to crash and the linebackers will be trapped inside.

If Kansas State stuffs the interior run, I’m not sure Washington State has a plan B. They didn’t last week.

In short, stuff the run, make Pinnick throw the ball, and don’t lose focus on the back end and cut someone loose deep and I don’t see a way forward for the West Coast Cats from Pullman.

Wildcats > Cougars in my humble opinion.

item.title: D’Andre Swift signing hefty $33.75 million Bears extension
item.description: The deal includes $27.5 million guaranteed and keeps the veteran running back in Chicago through the 2029 season.
item.content:encoded:
Bears fans and fantasy football general managers will be happy to know that D’Andre Swift isn’t going anywhere anytime soon.

The Bears agreed to a three-year, $33.75 million contract extension with Swift on Friday, according to ESPN’s Adam Schefter.

The deal includes $27.5 million guaranteed and keeps the veteran running back in Chicago through the 2029 season.

It’s a significant commitment to Swift and a heavy investment in the running back position, which is always something that’ll garner attention in today’s NFL.

Swift, 27, was entering the final season of the three-year, $24 million contract he signed with Chicago in 2024.

But after his best season in the NFL, the Bears are committing to Swift, even after selecting Kyle Monangai — who had a strong rookie campaign — in the seventh round of last year’s draft.

In 2025, Swift rushed for a career-high 1,087 yards and nine touchdowns on 223 carries, averaging 4.9 yards per attempt. He also impacted the passing game, catching 34 receptions for 299 yards and another touchdown while being a check-down option for the blossoming Caleb Williams.

Monangai recorded 169 carries for 783 rushing yards and five touchdowns on the ground, while adding 18 catches for 164 yards and a receiving TD.

The Bears finished third in the NFL with 2,456 rushing yards last season, led by Swift and Monangai, en route to their first NFC North title since 2018.

Last season, the Bears also won their first playoff game since 2010, coming on top in a dramatic 31-27 wild-card round encounter with the rival Packers before falling to the Rams in an equally heart-stopping 20-17 overtime game in the divisional round.

Previously, Swift enjoyed stints with the Eagles in 2023 and the Lions — who selected him in Round 2 of the 2020 NFL Draft — from 2020-22.

Swift’s lone Pro Bowl honor came as a member of the Eagles three seasons ago, when he rushed for 1,049 yards on 229 carries and five touchdowns.
